articles.title: New Hallcon Contract Raises Wages, Improves Safety
articles.content: On October 12, members of UE Locals 155, 977, 1077, 1177, and 1477 voted overwhelmingly to ratify a new four-year national collective bargaining agreement with their employer, Hallcon Inc. Base wages will increase between 11 and 25 percent over the duration of the contract. In the first year, most wages will increase between five and 10 percent. Hallcon is one of three main companies hired by the Class I freight railroads to transport rail crews within and between rail yards. Some UE members work as yard drivers, whose work is shifted and generally occurs within the confines and surroundings of a railyard. Others work as road drivers, who transport crews on an as-needed basis for the railroad, typically in long-haul trips. The new agreement, which is the third national master contract between the UE and Hallcon, covers drivers living everywhere from the country’s largest cities — Chicago, Los Angeles, Houston — to some of its most remote rural towns — places like Vaughn, NM, Keddie, CA, and International Falls, MN. Five UE locals are party to the contract, four of which exclusively represent rail crew transportation drivers. UE Local 1177 represents drivers in the Midwest and UE Local 977 represents drivers in the South, while Hallcon drivers in California, New Mexico, and New Jersey are represented by UE Locals 1077, 1477, and amalgamated Local 155 respectively. The UE bargaining committee began to prepare for negotiations in January of 2026, and officially kicked off bargaining in late June. Less than two months later, on August 16, UE Local 977 President Nandell Baines , a member of the bargaining committee, passed away after a hard-fought battle with cancer. She died just two days before scheduled bargaining in her hometown of Houston. Drivers in Baines’ local, Local 977, are the lowest-paid drivers in the national bargaining unit. Bargaining committee member and Local 1077 President Diana Martinez said that after Baines passed, “the bargaining committee resolved to make sure that Local 977’s members won big in the contract, even if their local didn’t have an actual seat at the bargaining table during the last month and a half of negotiations.” They were successful in meeting this goal: drivers in Local 977 won the largest wage gains in the entire contract, including immediate gains of 13 percent in Louisiana. “The new raise is going to help all of us employees down South”, said Local 977 Recording Secretary Chyrl Davis . “It’s going to mean more income in our pockets.” Beyond base wages, drivers won gains to paid time off, night and weekend shift differentials, and cell phone reimbursement pay. Notably, this new contract provides road drivers, whose hours are not guaranteed, with much-needed relief in the form of a biweekly bonus simply for accepting trips and driving safely. Every pay period, drivers who meet trip acceptance and safety criteria will pocket an additional $100, on top of wages earned by driving for the company. This creates some much-needed consistency, since road drivers’ take-home pay was previously determined entirely by how many hours they worked. “Road drivers in my area have been dealing with fluctuating hours for too long”, said Lauren Sims , Los Angeles Area Chief Steward for Local 1077 and bargaining committee member. “Now, road drivers will get a bonus for accepting the calls they do get, even if not many calls come in that week.” The CBA also includes improved workplace safety language. Because Hallcon’s vehicles run round-the-clock, they are prone to mechanical issues that occasionally raise serious safety concerns. UE Local 1477 steward and Western Region executive board member Ray Silva appreciates new language that ensures drivers continue to get paid if they refuse to drive an unsafe van: “The new CBA does a lot more for our safety,” he says. The union successfully defeated company attempts to dilute the grievance procedure and disciplinary protections. According to Local 1177 Chief Steward and bargaining committee member Clarence Hill , “We told the company that unless it stops unfairly disciplining drivers without due process, and starts responding to grievances in a timely manner, we had no reason to defang our contract language.” None of these wins came without a fight. Hallcon made sure to constantly remind the union that the railroads were threatening to outsource more work to Uber, Lyft, or other transportation contractors. “They even lectured us about how gas prices affected their bottom line, as if gas prices aren’t also affecting us”, said Erin Frimpong , Local 1177 Chief Steward and bargaining committee representative. Drivers called the company’s bluff; even with a tight economy, Hallcon could share more of the wealth. In early August, over 200 UE members surprised Hallcon representatives by logging onto the Zoom bargaining session to witness the company provide its first economic counterproposal. Then, drivers organized a series of bannering events at railyards across the country, alerting the railroads that they meant business. In the final days of the contract fight, hundreds of drivers signed a strike pledge. Along with Davis and Silva, UE 1077 San Bernardino Area Chief Steward Jaime Valencia was one of over 200 UE members who played a role in organizing their coworkers while the bargaining committee travelled around the country for negotiations. Valencia says that he is personally proud of the work that he and his coworkers put into their contract campaign. Although he is satisfied with the final contract, he acknowledges that it is not perfect. After ratification, Valencia said, “Our fight for better wages, benefits, and working conditions does not end here. We will continue organizing, strengthening our membership, and preparing to fight for an even stronger contract in 2030.” The UE Bargaining Committee consisted of Nandell Baines, Local 977, Diana Martinez and Lauren Sims, Local 1077, and Miya Bell , Erin Frimpong, Clarence Hill, and Larry Hopkins , Local 1177. They were assisted by Field Organizer Noah Wexler . Staff Coordinator J Burger and Field Organizer Fred Hatef provided additional support during negotiations and throughout the contract campaign. articles.title: To Feed the Hungry: The Merit of Charity
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: By Asanti M. To recount the history of the human struggle against hunger is to see a true virtue birthed from necessity in its most basic form. From time immemorial cooperation precluded death; community cemented life; and collaboration rose as the principal weapon against hunger. To stave off the constant assault on our mortality, collective structures arose from collective needs. Both calculated and spontaneous efforts set in motion the systematic destruction of our innate enemy and laid the foundation for a solidarity rooted in a visceral understanding of the human condition. Rather than eliminate hunger, contemporary modes of societal organization produce social structures that justify material dispossession. Collaboration has been abandoned for competition, and hunger is given space to thrive beyond the immediate consequences of climate or natural disasters. The sympathy that surrounds the suffering fades into a background colored with the constant tragedies that make up the white noise of modern life. Here in the States, there are countless organizations that endeavor to feed the hungry, yet every day a child starves. The tireless efforts of the charitable grant little solace to a mother whose labor can’t support her child nor to a father whose determinations fall short of supplying even the bare necessities. This struggle isn’t unique to the innocent but oppresses the “blameworthy” all the same. People deemed guilty by our systems are forced to navigate a world entirely unsympathetic to their plight. Despite the commonality of their condition, we see the suffering separated into two distinct categories: on one hand we have the fetishization of the hungry that abstracts their social position to maintain the image of an idealized victim; while on the other, we witness their unabated condemnation as inept failures or criminals on the margins of society. Each rendition subtracts from their humanity and masks the innately human battle against hunger. The “innocent” are allotted systematically constrained charity while the others are left to face an unforgiving material and social degradation. It’s not difficult to understand the sympathy that stirs the charitable. Their imagination brings the extremity of the idealized victim to the forefront of their mind: the emaciated frames, the protruding ribs, the sunken cheeks. They aptly discern what an all-consuming force the fiend we call Hunger can be, and, with heart in hand, they motion to alleviate the suffering of its victims. Their sympathy materializes in both simple and elaborate structures of food distribution, supplementing the diets of millions and temporarily subduing the otherwise relentless pains of starvation. The admirable solution posited by the sympathetic addresses the immediate needs of the hungry but does so under the unabated pretense of a deeply entrenched meritocratic framework that constricts its application. As the hungry toil, the meritocratic ethic that asserts: an individual deserves neither reward nor punishment from factors beyond their control, casts a moral fog over our deeply disturbing distribution of wealth. Hunger, death, and destitution become accepted as viable individual outcomes, rather than deeply opposed as communal ails. The elimination of hunger ceases to be one of the fundamental cornerstones of organized society and gives way to the social inversion that elevates the accumulation of individual wealth above collective humanity. The meritocratic ideal operates as an ostensibly unbiased sorting mechanism leaving the supposed listless to languish while the prudent rise to pinnacle of their aspirations. In our case, the ideal that exists in the national consciousness never escapes the imagination; all manner of happenstance, prejudice, or generic biases that color the human psyche render our “meritocracy” nominally absurd and functionally inept. Nevertheless, the mockery goes to serve as a retroactive justification for the languid position of the hungry, consequently molding the contours of the discussions surrounding their humanity. Conversations and solutions alike are fixed on optimizing the performance of the poor, while utterly disregarding the simple fact that our nation decorates landfills with several billions of pounds of wasted food every month. Wealthy institutions harp on charity, the unidirectional and placid rendition of mutual aid, but rarely engage in the opposition required to dismantle the sorting system itself. Our make-believe meritocracy shrouds the public imagination and replaces any concept of common humanity with fictitious barriers used to justify the vast disparities inherent to our current system. Any talk of universal dignity by the charitable is reduced to platitudinal posturing when the systems that place profit over the abolition of hunger go unquestioned. The moral logic that permeates our nominally meritocratic society seamlessly accomplishes the impossible task of nullifying history and rendering structural social context irrelevant. The mirage of potential upward social mobility acts as the comforting illusion that instills hope against the foreboding backdrop of uncertainty. Blind individual perseverance is brutely applied as the universal answer to all societal ails and erodes the need for any deeper use of contextual evaluation. Wealth becomes proof of productivity and productivity rises to the status of virtue. Conversely, any outward semblance of economic strife, if not refuted as transient, becomes evidence of personal failure. The excess of the wealthy in the face of poverty doesn’t spur moral condemnation because meritocratically the excess is evidence of the assumed judicious character of the well-off. The impoverished, on the other hand, can bear no such virtue, evidenced by their very condition. There’s no need to understand the complex sociopolitical realities that produce poverty and hunger, because hunger itself ceases to be a collective social issue framed by laws, polices, history and the like. But rather reduces to the sole burden of the individual, in which the failure to provide or produce equates to the moral failure ascribed to poverty. The moral judgment befalling the impoverished is only allowed redemption through the accumulation of status and wealth in the free market. By extension, the public’s measure of our own dignity degrades into a measure of our market value disregarding any innate human essence or even our societal contributions. Arbitrations of the market, buffered by charity, define the dynamic in which hunger is justified while the rules created by the free market masquerade as the only path forward, cementing isolation and competition as a seemingly natural default. The imposition of this isolating ethos shreds the collective call to abolish hunger into millions of fragmented families struggling to toil their way through an inherently dehumanizing system. Any motion towards solidarity becomes a tortured struggle that opposes the fundamental assumptions that form the bedrock of a fractured society. In a nation where the market determines humanity and a feigned meritocracy casts a veil over its manufactured borders between our brothers and sisters, the claim that “not a soul should starve if there is enough food to be had” seems the crazed cry of a radical. The post To Feed the Hungry: The Merit of Charity first appeared on Red Fault .

articles.title: The Local: Nov. 12, 2026 news roundup
articles.author: The NYC Local - NYC DSA Labor Working Group
articles.content: Welcome back to The Local, a publication of NYC-DSA Labor Working Group reporting every two weeks. Send any tips, corrections, and other feedback to thenyclocal@substack.com. In this issue, Mayor Mamdani might be trying to get a progressive union leader to run in 2028, a Cornell study finds that private equity was able to enter and consolidate the home health care industry in New York state due to weak regulation, which also dialectically left it susceptible to one big unionization push by 1199SEIU, and the NYC Ferry unionization drive with TWU propels forward (please drop us a tip with more ferry puns in case this continues, as we are starting to run out). Photo credit: Alexandra Chan at Marcela’s canvass 10/24. Organizing Workers at shelter and supportive housing nonprofit Lantern Community Services are organizing with AFSCME DC37 and demanding voluntary recognition. Editorial employees at Scientific American voted 20-1 to join the Writers Guild of America East. Production assistants at CBS Studios working on the show “Elsbeth” voted 27-0 to join LIUNA Local 724. A unit of postdoc associates and senior postdoc associates at the technically private Research Foundation for the State University of New York located at Stony Brook University voted 92-1 to join the Communications Workers of America. Workers at Adapt Community Network are organizing with the UFT Local 2. The unit of workers at JFK contractors Unifi Aviation we reported on in the last issue filed another representation petition to organize with the TWU. The unionization drive at NYC Ferry continues as a unit of deckhands and senior deckhands organizes with the TWU. Two units of workers at City Squash in the Bronx are organizing as the City Squash Staff Union. Workers at the NYU Langone Sunset Terrace FHC are organizing with 1199SEIU. Workers at LaGuardia Airport contractor Oxford Airport Technical Services are organizing with the International Union of Operating Engineers Local 30. Bargaining & Action The New York Live Arts Workers Union voted to authorize a strike . The Association of Legislative Employees held a lunchtime picket for Legislative division bargaining. Brooklyn nurse and union leader Sarah Dowd, who was suspended without pay by H+H management for holding organizing meetings with nurses on her day off, has been reinstated with full back pay . City Hall A Public Employment Relations Board judge sided with the UFT and found that the city’s Department of Education illegally hired three non-union paraprofessionals at a Bronx elementary school in 2023. [The Chief Leader] Albany The MTA unilaterally cancelled a benefit under which workers who had used more than 50 percent of their sick days could cash them out at retirement in a lump sum payment, leaving the benefit only for workers who had used less than half of their sick days. Workers argued that the unilateral move will, if anything, worsen absenteeism because, past a certain point, it no longer becomes worth it for workers to save their sick days. [The Chief Leader] Two studies released this year by the Cornell University School of Industrial and Labor Relations found that the state’s weak regulatory landscape for home health care allowed private equity to infiltrate the sector, especially when the private equity-backed Public Partnerships LLC was given the contract to administer over half the state’s home health care services. But ironically, the same consolidation has made it possible for 1199SEIU to unionize the 200,000-member workforce in one swoop. [The Chief Leader] Miscellaneous Mayor Mamdani has been meeting with progressive union leaders like Jimmy Williams Jr. (IUPAT), Sara Nelson (AFA-CWA), and Shawn Fain (UAW) to potentially recruit a presidential candidate for 2028. [Axios] The Democratic wave of election victories last Tuesday may, in the near term, pave the way for state and local legislative reforms that benefit workers. articles.title: New York’s Blue Wave Results & Public Dissatisfaction with Democratic Leadership
articles.author: The Thorn - NYC DSA Electoral Working Group
articles.content: The Thorn is published weekly by the Electoral Working Group of the NYC Democratic Socialists of America . Join the Electoral Working Group ! Local News Since last week’s midterms, there has been widespread public outcry against the feckless Democratic leadership of Hakeem Jefferies and Chuck Schumer, with calls for them to make way for a more progressive/offensive leader. A Change.org petition has circulated, calling for Hakeem Jefferies to step down as prospective House Speaker for the incoming 120th Congress. It currently sits at over one million signatures. A likewise petition exists for Chuck Schumer to step down as prospective Senate Majority Leader, though it only boasts approx. one hundred thousand signatures. This outcry has also spread to Senate electeds and incumbents , including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Abdul El-Sayed and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, and Julianna Stratton of Illinois. Despite the backlash, however, Schumer remains intent with maintaining his role as majority leader. According to New York City Criminal Summons, a recently published data analysis reveals that the NYPD names East New York and the South Bronx as neighborhoods most liable for low-level criminal summons, such as loitering, panhandling, and loitering. Attorney General Letitia James won a lawsuit against Nassau County Executive & Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman over his countywide ban on transgender people in sports. This lawsuit was filed in July 2024 after the ban was passed, and the verdict comes one day after Blakeman’s loss in the gubernatorial race. In the aftermath of Cornell University’s controversial revelation alleging a gang rape incident involving seven fraternity students, the school’s faculty senate votes “no-confidence” in its leadership. Governor Hochul signed S9051B, a law that calls on state regulation and protection against “companion bots” that are engaged with by minors. Election News New York Governor Kathy Hochul secured her reelection bid by a twenty-point margin over Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman. This includes notable flips from Rockland, Nassau, and Suffolk Counties, who previously voted for Republican gubernatorial candidate Lee Zeldin in 2022. Mamdani-backed DSA candidates Claire Valdez and Daraliza Avila Chevalier won their House races in the 7th and 13th congressional districts, respectively. In New York’s 17th congressional district, Democratic candidate Cait Conley defeats Republican incumbent Mike Lawler. New York City voters approved all five ballot proposals to overhaul and streamline changes within the city government. The proposals were in regard to: Question 1: Streamlining the approval process for private usage of public spaces. Question 2: Reducing paperwork for businesses and nonprofits seeking city contracts. Question 3: Changes to street sweeping projects combined with reforms to city-owned and government properties. Question 4: Simplify construction processes by establishing a centralized system for applicants to navigate approvals across city agencies. Question 5: Addressing how much money New York City should set aside for future emergencies.

articles.title: On Brandon Johnson: Party Building & The Meaning of Socialist Governance
articles.author: Groundwork Towards a Socialist Future
articles.source: Building Up: The Groundwork DSA Blog - Groundwork: Towards a Socialist Future
articles.content: Why Chicago DSA Should Not Endorse Brandon Johnson Author: Chicago Groundwork Brandon Johnson is seeking Chicago DSA’s endorsement after a politically fraught first term. Soon the chapter will have to weigh in on if we will lend support to Mayor Johnson and what that support looks like. This question is not an easy one, as Brandon has been a key champion of many legislative priorities for Chicago DSA. Still, endorsing or recommending Brandon runs the risk of tying ourselves to a deeply unpopular incumbent and a failed model of progressive governance, all the while the DSA model is proving itself across the country. Instead, we should use this cycle to triple down on the Socialist Slate, agitate around our Workers Deserve More platform, and build towards a socialist mayoral run in 2031. How we got here In 2023, it was heavily rumored that then-candidate Brandon Johnson might seek CDSA’s endorsement. He was a labor, CTU candidate running as a progressive, and it became clear early on that Congressman Chuy Garcia was not going to run the type of class struggle election his record as congressmen might suggest. The Brandon coalition was a mighty one. Union giants like CTU and SEIU alongside nearly all the progressive ward-level organizations were consolidated into an organization called United Working Families. This whole coalition was all in for Brandon, and it became clear that Johnson would hold the left's mantle in this election. Chatter emerged within the chapter about whether or not to endorse Brandon along factional lines. This conflict became so public that eventually Brandon’s team reached out to DSA leaders and asked that the chapter not endorse him. Many members of the chapter who had organized in IPOs at the time that supported Brandon had severed their ties with the organization and began organizing within their IPOs full-time. Brandon Johnson would go on to win the election and beat Paul Vallas with a working class coalition largely thanks to mobilizations from United Working Families. CDSA would continue to go the entire cycle without having either a chapter-wide discussion on Brandon Johnson or establishing a position on how to deal with his administration once he won. This was a major failure we cannot repeat. The years that have followed have not been great for Johnson. Though Johnson has some wins, such as expanding the Chicago CARE program, his administration has been plagued with setbacks. One of Johnson’s first challenges was dealing with the migrant crises. Between the end of Lori Lightfoot’s term and the beginning of the Johnson administration, over 50,000 migrants were bussed from Texas to Chicago on the orders of Texas Governor Greg Abbot. The response to this crisis was messy. Migrants were living in rat-infested shelters, and many were sent to shelters in neighborhoods that did not have adequate services. Even still, for some Black Chicagoans it felt as though the new Black mayor was helping the migrants while their needs were going unmet. Though Johnson’s initial pledge to house the migrants was admirable, it split the Black and Latino coalition that helped him get elected. Johnson’s landmark housing proposal, Bring Chicago Home, was also defeated only a year after the mayor’s election. Things would only get harder for the mayor. A turf war between CTU and SEIU has turned a key allied union of Johnson into an adversary. This has played out most visibly this year, with SEIU backing mostly rival, charter-school-funded candidates against CTU’s endorsed slate, putting forward and winning an alternative Board of Education President candidate. SEIU has now also endorsed Alexi Gennioulous, the current frontrunner in the mayoral race. Present Day Today, both the organizational coalition that brought the mayor to power, as well as his coalition to pass legislation on the City Council have faltered. Whereas early in the mayor’s term he was able to secure significant wins, such as abolishing the tipped minimum wage and banning ShotSpotter, today he’s marching closer to a veto-proof majority in the city council. Major initiatives like last year's Corporate Head Tax or the Protecting Renters Ordinance have stalled or failed. Even previous wins, such as One Fair Wage or the banning of Shot Spotter are showing signs of reversing. In many respects, the mayor doesn’t have the popular mandate, the on-the-ground organizational support, or the coalition left in the city council to enact transformative policy for the Chicago working class, nor do the prospects for his re-election look favorable. Though we welcome Johnson’s shift to class-based messaging since the beginning of Trump’s second term and his attempts to make inroads with Chicago DSA, such moves should be weighed in the context that all of this is a last-ditch effort to salvage a fraught administration by tying itself to DSA, which has elected the mayor of America’s two largest cities in just under two years. Why endorsement does not make sense The last four years have demonstrated the limits of a left-labor coalition that is divorced from democratic organization and a socialist critique of capitalism. Some proponents of endorsement may think that DSA is the missing key to this puzzle or that endorsing Brandon brings opportunities that may not currently be present to DSA. Much of this rush to endorse Brandon is based on excitement that figures like Zohran have brought to New York City politics and the stunning results of the 2026 midterm election. Still, these perceived benefits pale in comparison to the downsides of endorsing Brandon. The case against endorsing Brandon Johnson can be broken down into the following reasons: This is not a DSA difference Campaign Johnson’s low approval among working class Chicagoans outweigh the potential upside of endorsement Endorsing Johnson clouds the benefits of socialist governance Not a DSA Difference Campaign Brandon Johnson is not a socialist, nor is he a member of Chicago DSA. DSA’s growth and influence, particularly over the last 2 years, has been a result of running people who are willing to join DSA and proudly proclaim themselves as democratic socialists. This isn’t a sectarian requirement; it is essential to party building. We want politicians who see the electoral cycle as bigger than themselves and the importance of having an organizational home in DSA. It is also vital that our candidates call themselves socialists. Running as an open socialist means putting a stake in the ground and saying that you are for working-class, democratic control of the economy. It’s a significant marker indicating that the candidate opposes the exploitative, extractive, and oppressive nature of capital and will stand firmly on the side of the working class. It also draws a line publicly between socialists and capitalists in the eyes of the masses, which is crucial to our political project. Drawing that line is important for both trust, building our party, and building our movement. Candidates like Zohran help make socialism acceptable to the masses. These elections become bigger than one particular candidate or one particular office. Retreating on this not only sacrifices our ability to grow from our electoral interventions, it puts the needs of one election cycle and one politician above the socialist movement. The negatives of endorsing a non-socialist are magnified by the reality of DSA being a very junior coalition partner in this race. We won’t have any leverage to determine the platform, field strategy, messaging, fundraising goals, or any other element of the campaign. We would essentially be campaigning for a candidate who can flip on key issues like ShotSpotter with little ability for us to push him to change directions. Depending on how the campaign is run, such an outcome could be harmful to DSA’s reputation if Johnson makes pivots to the right. While we don’t always need to be a senior coalition partner, being a junior coalition partner can be mitigated by supporting a candidate who is openly socialist and is polarizing voters along class lines. Throughout the country, DSA has risen to prominence as a powerful force in American politics by running candidates in competitive races with the aim to win, running open socialists who are members of DSA, and running races where DSA can be the senior coalition partner. These sorts of campaigns are known as the DSA Difference and have led to the rapid growth of DSA. A campaign not being a DSA Difference campaign is not disqualifying in and of itself so long as the candidates are socialist. Without that, running these types of races risks cheapening the DSA endorsement, stagnating growth, and, at worst, risking DSA’s reputation. Johnson’s Unfavorables A common reason for endorsing Brandon Johnson is that it will help us build with Black voters on the South and West Side. One serious limiter to this proposition is Johnson’s poor favorables. Brandon Johnson currently sits at a 22% approval rating. If that negative approval was led by exclusively white voters on the North Side, the argument that we can build with Black Chicagoans city-wide could hold water. However, Johnson’s approval is sitting at 2 4% with Black Chicagoans . His approval also sits at 23% on the South Side, and just around 22% on the West Side. To put that into perspective, this overall approval rating is 8 points lower than Trump’s and is lower than George W. Bush after the 2008 financial crisis. Brandon’s unpopularity seriously threatens the working class coalitions we can form in these areas ourselves through our normal campaign work. Currently, doors are being knocked right now on the South Side for Raheem. We are building these inroads ourselves as DSA through our own hard work in areas like the 3rd ward. Furthermore, it's wrong to assume that just because a candidate is the Black candidate in the race, that said candidate will win a large share of Black votes. The data suggests that Johnson has work to do within these communities himself. It does not help DSA make inroads in these communities to campaign for a candidate who has lost significant support within the same constituency. The argument that we can use this to build on the South and West sides further falls apart with the reality being that if we endorse Johnson, we are largely going to be canvassing for him in the same areas we are already running candidates. If we don’t, we run the risk of spreading our field program thin and losing the elections we have already committed to. Since we will largely be dual canvassing, there isn’t much opportunity to build with voters on the South Side outside of what we are already doing with Raheem. Clouding the benefits of socialist governance On the surface, it may seem like there are few tangible differences between the governing philosophies of Zohran and Johnson. Both are housing advocates, both support workers' rights and labor, and both believe in taxing the rich. However, there is a key distinct difference in their model of governance. Zohran has prioritized a model of government whose key priority is deliverance, while Brandon has prioritized a government that is based on being representative. This passage in Zohran’s inaugural address perfectly summarizes his approach to governance. “In writing this address, I have been told that this is the occasion to reset expectations, that I should use this opportunity to encourage the people of New York to ask for little and expect even less. I will do no such thing. The only expectation I seek to reset is that of small expectations. Beginning today, we will govern expansively and audaciously. We may not always succeed. But never will we be accused of lacking the courage to try. To those who insist that the era of big government is over, hear me when I say this—no longer will City Hall hesitate to use its power to improve New Yorkers’ lives. For too long, we have turned to the private sector for greatness, while accepting mediocrity from those who serve the public. I cannot blame anyone who has come to question the role of government, whose faith in democracy has been eroded by decades of apathy. We will restore that trust by walking a different path—one where government is no longer solely the final recourse for those struggling, one where excellence is no longer the exception. We expect greatness from the cooks wielding a thousand spices, from those who stride out onto Broadway stages, from our starting point guard at Madison Square Garden. Let us demand the same from those who work in government. In a city where the mere names of our streets are associated with the innovation of the industries that call them home, we will make the words ‘City Hall' synonymous with both resolve and results.” Zohran has an ideological commitment to a government that delivers for workers above all else, a government of excellence. New York City's government had long been hollowed out. Many core city functions were outsourced to contractors, private companies, and nonprofits. Furthermore, many employees within government were patronage employees. Immediately, Zohran sought to transform New York City Government through hiring staff with movement and policy expertise, cutting consultant contracts, and centralizing formerly outsourced projects back within city government, building state capacity. One of the first things Zohran did was clearing house of the old Adam’s appointees and senior employees by asking 179 staffers for their resignation before taking office. He conducted a country-wide public search for professionals, receiving over 80,000 applications. Zohran would eventually hire over 149 new staffers, essentially transforming leadership in City Hall. Many of these hires consisted of policy professionals who have a track record of delivering, like in the case of Lina Khan, or a deep expertise in the subject matter they are dealing with, like housing justice appointee Cea Weaver. Outside of initial hiring, Zohran has used his executive authority to expand government capacity. Just this year he launched The Civil Service Modernization Advisory Committee, which is a joint project with labor unions to speed up the hiring process and place people in good paying city government jobs. Projects like the Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) seek to make government more responsive to working class needs, by doing a full scale audit of government agencies to remove outdated barriers that slow down infrastructure projects and delivering services, ensuring that agencies have proper enforcement mechanisms, as well as saving money by reducing redundancies. This type of government reform has historically been monopolized by the right for privatization and austerity, but Zohran is using this model to both make government more equipped to respond to the needs of New York City's working class, as well as saving the city money, which can be used for more programs. Under this model of governance, no problem is too small. Zohran has made it a show to fix potholes submitted through an online portal (or over social media), assembled an army of snow shovelers to tackle the first major winter storm of his administration, and even purchased thousands of sports tickets for fans of major sporting events. The concept of a government that relentlessly works to deliver for the working class in the way that Zohran has shown is a direct byproduct of his socialist politics. The blueprint for much of what underpins his governing philosophy can be found in how the Milwaukee sewer socialists governed. Such governance has proven to be popular and is a great differentiator in the use of executive power between socialist executives and more progressive ones. Rebuilding state capacity, rather than outsourcing it to non-profits, is the hallmark that distinguishes socialist municipal governance from progressive municipal governance. This model of governance is in direct contrast to Brandon Johnson. Chicago has had a long history of patronage politics, largely due to the machine politics nature that has underpinned much of the city's history. Brandon Johnson’s first move was to retain much of Lori Lightfoot's old administrative staff. He kept over 55% of Lori’s former hires. Johnson would then fill in his own appointments with movement and labor leaders, as well as leaders of the clergy. One of Johnson’s recent appointments to the CTA board Rev. Ira Acree did not have transit experience, nor was a current rider of the CTA. He even struggled to answer basic questions during Johnson’s city hall hearing. Rev. Ira Acree was a key Johnson supporter during his 2023 election and is the senior pastor at Greater St John Bible Church of Chicago. Though the former example is a rather extreme case, the Johnson administration has not shown a similar priority as the Mamdani administration in hiring based on expertise. The Johnson model of staffing largely prioritizes community and movement leaders, and sometimes substituting experience within the movement for relevant subject expertise. Johnson has also continued the model of outsourcing city functions, rather than to private contractors to nonprofit groups. City initiatives are often done through public grants which are overseen by his administration but executed through the nonprofit sector. A prime example of this is his Green Social Housing initiative, which is being executed through a publicly owned nonprofit instead of the government building social housing. The key differences between the Zohran and Brandon form of governance is that Zohran’s starts with the question of how we can execute power, using the state, on behalf of workers, whereas Johnson’s key question is who has a seat at the table. While elements of Johnson’s governing philosophy are important, prioritizing representation at the expense of execution has hurt the administration's ability to deliver. Both of these governing philosophies are represented by the coalitions that brought them to power. For Zohran, it was largely DSA, a singularly ideologically coherent group with a specific program. For Brandon, it was a coalition of neighborhood and labor organizations. Representing the interests of such a broad coalition can make it hard to have a coherent government philosophy, as well as cohering a durable coalition, which has largely faltered in the case of Johnson. We have now seen these two models of executive governance in execution, and both have had wildly different results. Zohran is nearing 70% approval rating almost a year into his term, while Johnson is at 22%. Endorsing Johnson flattens these distinctions and will make it harder to differentiate our candidates and our approach from the currently unpopular model that has been executed under Johnson. Furthermore, it risks all the momentum DSA has built from running winning campaigns over the last year. Should Johnson lose with a DSA endorsement, the tail of Chicago will be used as a warning against socialist governance for years to come. No to Recommendation With all the downsides of a Johnson endorsement, one might ask, why not just a statement affirming our support for Brandon Johnson? Such a statement is unlikely to be read by the public as anything short of an endorsement. It further complicates things under a potentially secured memorandum of understanding from the Johnson administration. This memorandum would give Chicago DSA a seat on Johnson’s Youth Outreach Committee, as well as a table at all of Johnson’s church events on the South and West Side. It even creates a data-sharing agreement that will share the campaigns data just for the cycle. This MOU puts the chapter in a weird place with just a recommendation. We’d be actively tabling at Johnson campaign events and would be in charge of his youth outreach, yet if anyone asked us DSA’s position we’d have to explain that he is not a DSA endorsed candidate and that we are not campaigning for him, a position that is contradictory to hold. The Way Forward Chicago Groundwork is bringing forward two resolutions that seek to chart a way forward. One, titled Chicago Deserves More , seeks to have us conduct an anti-campaign against Alexi Giannoulias, the neoliberal, corporate-backed candidate in the race, and against Susanna Mendoza, who is running the furthest-right campaign in the race. It would have us rebuild our comms capacity by working on a targeted campaign to agitate against these two candidates using Workers Deserve More. The resolution also combines efforts with our street agitprop team calling for wheat pasting and flyering of anti-Alexi and Mendoza literature across the city. Chicago Deserves More also sets an ambitious goal of building the chapter towards a mayoral run of our own in 2031. The second piece of the Groundwork-slated proposals, ABCs of Socialism , seeks to create a ranked voter guide. This voter guide will rank all the candidates in the municipal cycle, and will issue out letter grades ranging from B to F based on alignment with our Workers Deserve More Platform. Only our endorsed candidates will receive a letter grade of A. The second part of this is printing out literature with Workers Deserve More on one side and a QR code linking to our voter guide on the other. This literature will be included in all canvasses for the socialist slate, and will help us grow our readership for our voter guide. Conclusion The excitement of elections such as Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman have sparked interest in being a part of a mayoral campaign. Chicago DSA is laying the groundwork for victories in February and even bigger victories in the years to come. By doubling down on our city council efforts and by negatively campaigning against the worst mayoral candidates we can build DSA into a party that can eventually contest power at the city level. Endorsing or recommending Johnson clouds this path. We encourage DSA members to support Chicago Deserves More and ABCs of Socialism to build DSA and work towards a socialist mayor in Chicago.

articles.title: Guglielmo Carchedi Was a Pathbreaking Marxist Economist
articles.author: Joseph Choonara
articles.content: In October, the radical left lost Guglielmo Carchedi — “Mino” to his friends and comrades — who died in his sleep at the age of eighty-five. He was one of the great Marxist thinkers of our times. I first met him in London a few years after the economic meltdown of 2007–9, at a conference I organized for the journal International Socialism to explore the dynamics of that crisis. He spoke patiently and calmly, setting out his views with authority and an unwavering confidence in the power of Marxist theory. I heard him many more times over the next few years, always speaking with the same measured style. On occasion, he ended his presentations with a shy smile and the Latin “QED,” quod erat demonstrandum: “that which was to be demonstrated.” It was always a delight when our paths crossed. Often I would encounter him in conjunction with Michael Roberts , with whom Carchedi would form a close personal and intellectual relationship. The partnership was a fitting one. Roberts, himself a fine political economist, complemented Carchedi’s theoretical subtlety with a keen eye for a potential audience and a flair for showmanship, qualities long evident on Roberts’s indispensable blog . In turn, for Roberts, Carchedi was a mentor in the realm of dialectics and Marxist value theory. Together they produced a stream of articles; an edited collection, World in Crisis: A Global Analysis of Marx’s Law of Profitability ; and a coauthored book, Capitalism in the Twenty-first Century Through the Prism of Value . Carchedi was a kind and modest man, generous with his time when younger Marxists sought advice from him. He was refreshingly uninterested in whether those he spoke to worked in the academy or were simply left militants with a thirst for theory, as I was when we first met. He saw his work not merely as addressing a series of intellectual puzzles but as a contribution to the struggles of the working class. It is a great boon that new generations can continue to benefit from his wisdom through his writings. Here I will focus on some of his early contributions, which deserve broader appreciation. Middle-Class Problems The writing partnership with Roberts has helped win Carchedi a new readership. However, few among the younger generation of Marxists are aware of his early contributions to class theory, especially on the nature of the middle class. One of his first articles , “On the economic identification of the middle class,” appeared in 1975 in the journal Economy and Society . A second piece , “Reproduction of social classes at the level of production relations,” appeared in the same publication a couple of issues later. They would form two chapters of a book , On the Economic Identification of Social Classes . After much searching, I managed to get hold of a battered secondhand copy that North Staffordshire Polytechnic had marked “discarded from stock.” As with many niche academic texts of the period, the printers made the plates from the output of an electric typewriter. Only in 2024 did the publisher, Routledge, again make a facsimile of the text available. Carchedi’s contribution to class theory appeared in the shadow of better-known works by two authors grappling with similar problems. The first was the Greek-French Marxist Nicos Poulantzas, whose Classes in Contemporary Capitalism appeared in English in 1975. The second was Erik Olin Wright, whose first major foray into class theory, Class, Crisis and the State , appeared in 1978. Carchedi’s account, I would argue, offered a more convincing resolution than either of its major rivals. The new middle class has been a thorny problem for Marxist theory. Karl Marx saw capitalists and workers as the major contending classes within capitalism. He saw the former as the rulers of such societies and the latter as their potential adversaries, capable of overthrowing the rule of capital and beginning the process of forging a communist society. There was, Marx acknowledged, a substantial petty bourgeoisie, consisting of smallholders of capital, such as shopkeepers or artisans, along with their rural counterpart, the peasantry. Yet as capitalism came to predominate, it would, as Marx put it, “cut up” members of these groups “into two persons,” forcing them to adapt to the new society by operating as both capitalist and worker. There was no reason to imagine the petty bourgeoisie would vanish, but over long periods of time, the two key classes of capitalist society could begin to absorb such groups. This happens, for instance, when a peasant becomes successful enough to start hiring and exploiting wage labor. Conversely, it happens when a peasant can no longer reproduce themselves without turning to wage labor and subjecting themselves to exploitation at the hands of a capitalist. But where did this leave the new intermediate layers that modern capitalism created , such as the managers and supervisors that large enterprises required, or technicians and engineers? They worked for a wage, just like workers, but their role set them apart from the mass of wage labor. For some, this called into question the whole Marxist approach to class — or at least blurred beyond recognition the lines demarcating the classes of capitalism. Poulantzas had sought to resolve this issue by presenting a very restrictive conception of the working class, focused on “productive” workers (those who generate profit for capital) involved in creating material commodities. He assigned anyone who did not meet these criteria — service sector workers, those working in the sphere of circulation, and so on — to a “new petty bourgeoisie” on the grounds of their economic position. To this, he added “political” criteria, allowing him also to thrust managers into this new class, and “ideological” criteria, allowing him to add mental laborers. As Wright complained, Poulantzas’s approach would make about 70 percent of the US labor force of the time petty bourgeois, many of them on the grounds of ideology and politics. To regard, say, teachers or nurses as petty bourgeois seems particularly out of tune with today’s reality: such groups are clearly subject to the degrading power of capital and are often at the forefront of workplace struggle. Wright’s own alternative was to deal with these ambiguities through a notion of “objectively contradictory class locations,” avoiding forcing groups such as managers into either the class of capitalists or workers. However, Wright’s approach introduced a complication. He sought to apply his approach both to groups caught between capitalists and workers in the workplace, such as managers, and to other groups — semiautonomous wage-earners and small employers — he identified as lying between the traditional petty bourgeoisie and either workers or capitalists. This unnecessarily complicates the position of the petty bourgeoisie, whose very nature allows them to shade into the two major classes. The new middle class is a distinctive type of formation, requiring a different approach. Wright himself would come to reject elements of his earlier contribution. In his later work, he suggested that he had previously overemphasized criteria such as autonomy in identifying class locations at the expense of exploitation. However, from the mid-1980s, Wright increasingly drew on analytical Marxist thinkers such as John Roemer rather than on Marx’s own approach to exploitation. Roemer was skeptical of the value theory Marx developed in Capital , recasting exploitation as a matter of the different assets that individuals possess. As well as capitalist property, such assets could, in Wright’s new class model, be “organizational assets” or “skills.” The result was a fragmentation of the class structure, leading to myriad different class locations. Carchedi’s Alternative Carchedi offered a way out of this morass, drawing on Marx’s Capital . Groups such as managers in modern enterprises must perform two contradictory functions within capitalist production. These are not simply different technical functions; they are social functions, reflecting the imperatives of rival classes. On the one hand, managers perform some functions of the “collective worker,” including coordinating the labor process, something necessary in any large, complex workplace, in any type of society. On the other hand, they also perform “global functions of capital,” roles of control and surveillance necessary because the workplace sits within a class-divided society. As Carchedi wrote, they are a special group of waged employees forming a “hierarchically organized ensemble, “who collectively perform what used to be the function of an individual capitalist” alongside activities appropriate to the collective worker. These contradictory functions combine differently in different concrete jobs, influencing whether sections of the new middle class side with workers in struggle or align with their capitalist employers. The configuration of these functions is not static; it shifts with technological change, management culls, and restructurings. For those Marxists who paid attention, notably Bob Carter , Carchedi’s theory would form the basis for later work, both theoretical accounts of the new middle class and empirical studies of workplaces. It provided a missing link between the labor process analysis that Harry Braverman pioneered in the early 1970s and a sophisticated Marxist class theory. From Class to Value Carchedi’s early work on class may superficially seem disconnected from his later work on political economy. However, there are clear links. These become apparent in an exchange with Wright in 1989, which appeared in the collection The Debate on Classes . Here Carchedi criticized two elements of Wright’s methodology. The first was Wright’s embrace of analytical Marxism’s claim that there is no distinctive Marxist method, that the methods of mainstream social science will suffice. In place of this, Carchedi emphasized a dialectical approach. This meant acknowledging the crucial roles of social structures, which develop independent of the will of particular individuals. However, these structures are not static but subject to dynamism and change. This concern with method would persist. It is no coincidence that his 2011 book, Behind the Crisis , opens with a heading: “The need for dialectics.” Almost all of Carchedi’s major writings contain a discussion of method, emphasizing Marx’s dialectical standpoint. Second, Carchedi reasserted the centrality of Marx’s value theory. Here he would offer another pioneering contribution , as one of the progenitors, along with Alan Freeman and Andrew Kliman , of what its proponents came to call the Temporal Single System Interpretation of Marx. When analytical Marxists such as Roemer and Wright claimed Marx’s value theory was flawed, they were scrutinizing a modified version of the theory. For Carchedi, their approach drew heavily on an approach pioneered by figures such as Piero Sraffa, which revived elements of the approach of to the labor theory of value of Marx’s predecessor, David Ricardo. This “neo-Ricardianism” treated production not as a social and historical process but as a primarily technical one, in which a set of commodities gives rise to another set of commodities. The exploitation of labor ceases to play any distinctive role in creating new value. Neo-Ricardians, conceiving of the economy in this way, could model it through a set of simultaneous equations. As Carchedi pointed out, one of the key weaknesses in this approach was its neglect of the concept of time. Neo-Ricardians unrealistically assumed that the prices of the outputs of a given cycle of production were the same as the prices of the equivalent inputs into that cycle. Carchedi insisted on reintroducing time, following Marx in resisting seeing capitalism as a system in static equilibrium. One advantage to this approach was that it helped Carchedi to resolve what Marxists call the “transformation problem.” Marx’s Capital proposes that the value of commodities reflects the labor time that their production typically requires. This includes both the “living labor” of the workers producing them and the “dead labor,” the labor that workers expended in the past to create the material means of production that the process uses up. This had implications for the rate of profit, the ratio between profit and investment. For Marx, living labor had the distinctive role of creating new value. Because labor can do so in excess of the cost of its reproduction (the wage), this gives rise to profits. But because the ratio of living and dead labor varies between branches of the economy, Marx’s approach implied a different rate of profit in each. Yet even in Marx’s day, economists observed that profit rates tend to converge over time. Marx reconciled theory with reality through his transformation of values into “prices of production.” Capital migrates toward branches of the economy where profit rates are high, disrupting the price level as social demand and supply shift. Were this process to reach its conclusion, it would redistribute value between capitalists such that each receives the same average rate of profit on their investment. In fact, as Carchedi showed, this was only a tendency, and new disruptions upset any potential equilibrium long before the system could reach it. Many critics, starting with Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1896, followed by Ladislau von Bortkiewicz, Paul Sweezy, and Ian Steedman, have faulted Marx for considering only how this transformation of values into prices of production affects the outputs of production, without also transforming the value of inputs. For those working with an atemporal, equilibrium model, such as the neo-Ricardians, making this further transformation allowed them to detach the system of prices of production from value theory altogether. Carchedi argued that no such detachment was necessary. When capitalists obtain inputs for a new cycle of production, the value they advance is simply the price of production with which they left the previous cycle. This was what Carchedi termed their “social value.” Prices of production are, he proposed, not merely “determined by values but rather are their concrete form of existence.” Falling Profit Rates The hallmark of great Marxist political economy is to synthesize the often rather abstract discussions of value theory with an empirical understanding of a dynamic, changing, and crisis-prone system. This was very much on display in what I consider Carchedi’s finest work, Frontiers of Political Economy . Here Carchedi clarified and extended Marx’s approach in Capital while seeking to apply it to contemporary capitalism. The result is dazzling. Carchedi’s book deals with the intricacies of price formation in the context of uneven and complex processes of intercapitalist competition, first on the national terrain and then on a global scale, where, for instance, wage levels differ sharply. Besides the transformation problem discussed above, he investigated a range of controversies, such as precisely which forms of labor do and don’t produce value and how to account for different skill levels among workers. At the center of the book, a chapter on “Growth, crises, inflation and crashes” develops themes that would become prominent in his work. Here he focused on Marx’s “tendency of the rate of profit to fall” (TRPF). Capitalists must advance an ever-greater mass of capital, in the form of dead labor, to grab their share of the pool of profit that the system generates. But because only living labor generates new value, the scale of the employed workforce and the extent of its exploitation ultimately limit the size of this pool. The more dynamic capitalism is in mobilizing a greater amount of dead labor through automation and the expansion of capital, the more this tends to choke off future profits relative to investment, helping pave the way for crises. The TRPF has been a source of considerable controversy among Marxists. For some, it is an unnecessary distraction from value theory. For others, it is so hedged with counteracting tendencies that no one can grasp an overall pattern. For others still, the empirical evidence has falsified it. Carchedi argued that the TRPF should remain at the center of crisis theory. It was, he maintained, the ultimate expression of the contradictions of capitalism. This was because, as Marx had proposed, the very processes that impel capitalism forward — exploitation, competition, accumulation — can, through the TRPF, begin to undermine future accumulation. In his account, Carchedi acknowledged various counteracting tendencies, such as the intensification of exploitation from the 1980s, but argued that, in the long run, the TRPF overpowered these. It might also appear that financial expansion had injected new dynamism into capitalism. Yet for Carchedi, this reflected how the TRPF in productive sectors encouraged capital to shift into the sphere of finance, feeding speculative bubbles and ultimately financial crises. The meltdown of 2007–9 was not, in this account, a purely financial phenomenon but one ultimately rooted in the productive economy, the realm of workers’ exploitation and the site where their potential power concentrates. Carchedi’s Legacy I have only touched on a few elements of Carchedi’s contribution. His career saw him explore many other themes, ranging from the class nature of European integration to the relationship between value theory and artificial intelligence . It is far better that the interested reader consults such works for themselves to understand their richness and diversity. Doing so will also make clear the passion that motivated him. On that, let the final word go to Carchedi himself, from his acceptance speech on receiving the World Marxian Economics Award in 2021. Contrasting the 1960s and ’70s, a time of great hope for those on the radical left, with the present period, he said: An economic and financial crisis of major proportions is again knocking at the door; the destruction of our natural habitat proceeds unchecked; the divide between the poor of the world and the absurdly rich has never been so great; the dark clouds of a new world war are gathering on the horizon; right-wing ideologies resurrect and even fascism is raising its ugly face again. These are the dangers the new generations will have to face. The difficulties ahead for them will be immense. But the contradictory nature of the system is such that each time capitalism wins, the anti-capitalist forces regroup and counterattack with new forms of resistance. My hope is that my work will be of some help in their struggle. articles.title: Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: The 2026 midterms saw historic gains for socialists and progressives. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, the Democratic Party’s corporate wing is hurriedly spinning the result as a victory for centrists and “moderates.” Largely lost in this is the way that the Left has transformed what it actually means to run as a Democratic moderate or a centrist. Because looking at this year’s campaigns, there is no doubt that even the most uninspiring “moderate” candidates were taking several pages — whole chapters, really — from the books of Bernie Sanders, Zohran Mamdani, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. It’s worth recalling that before 2025, standard Democratic campaign rhetoric was all about “defending democracy,” railing against extremism and authoritarianism, and advocating for abortion rights — all good things on their merits, but (with the exception of abortion rights) largely abstract ones that are not as animating or as high a priority for the majority of voters as their basic pocketbook concerns. Just look at former President Joe Biden’s big kick-off speech for his reelection campaign, which was almost completely devoid of an economic message but heavy on talk of “MAGA extremists” and the “soul of America.” In fact, the absence of an economic message was a constant left-wing criticism of the party through the Biden era, including from this very magazine . This has now completely shifted. While Democratic candidates in 2024 ran by far most of their TV ads on abortion , with immigration coming a distant second, this year, the overwhelming focus of their ad spending was “affordability,” dropping $401 million on the topic — a full quarter of their $1.5 billion total spend. And where did the “affordability” frame come from? Well, both Democratic and Republican members of Congress happened to start spamming that word in their emails to constituents right after socialist Zohran Mamdani won the New York City Democratic primary with a campaign that put affordability at its very center. But it’s more than just coming up with a pithy new word describing voters’ struggles with the economy. A number of the moderate candidates who won in red states sounded oddly like Bernie Sanders, railing against billionaires and the ultrarich, the corrupting influence of money in politics, and swearing off corporate money. Senator-elect James Talarico called billionaires “the only minority destroying America.” (Antonio A. Esparza / CC BY-SA 4.0 ) The clearest example of this was Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, who said that the fundamental divide in US politics was “top versus bottom,” called billionaires “the only minority destroying America,” charged that “for fifty years, billionaire megadonors have been buying politicians” like his opponent who then “rig the rules of the economy,” and who said that “we already have class warfare in this country” in the form of “the billionaires waging war against the rest of us” — a line almost directly borrowed from Bernie Sanders. He was rewarded for it by winning by one of the biggest margins of the night and doing it in one of the reddest states in the country. The corporate center has tried to square this by simply retconning Talarico as one of them , a moderate , as Matthew Yglesias dubbed him. They point to the fact that he moved away from some of his support for trans rights, embraced an “all-of-the-above” energy policy, and eschewed Medicare for All in favor a public option (though the idea that’s a “centrist” or “moderate” policy would be surprising to anyone with a memory longer than five or six years). But even if Talarico wasn’t viewed by nearly half of all Texas voters as “very liberal” on the eve of the election (and as “somewhat liberal” by a further 27 percent), this is a pretty hard sell. To see why, look at Colin Allred. Just two years ago, Allred, a former NFL player, civil rights lawyer, and congressman, launched his own Texas Senate run with a campaign widely characterized as a “ centrist ” one against Republican Ted Cruz. What did that campaign involve? Allred cast the GOP as having become too extreme and told conservatives who believed in the rule of law and the Constitution that they should vote for him. He proudly touted his US Chamber of Commerce endorsement . He “was unable to successfully develop” an economic message against Cruz and made abortion and reproductive rights “ central to ” and the “ banner of ” his campaign instead. During their debate, he hammered Cruz for supporting an abortion ban and being soft on the January 6 rioters, calling him a “threat to democracy” and only offhandedly mentioning he cut taxes on the rich. Again, these are all important issues but were unconnected to voters’ economic struggles. The result: Cruz won by 8 points, nearly quadrupling his winning margin from six years earlier. Going Red in Red States This was not something unique to Texas and Talarico’s “moderate” campaign there. It was the case in every red state that Democrats just won a Senate seat in. Take a look at Annie Andrews’s campaign that made her the first Democrat elected to a South Carolina Senate seat in twenty-eight years . Andrews hammered her initial opponent, the late Lindsey Graham, for “sell[ing] out to big money” and for being “willing to take food off our kids’ plates” and gut Medicaid “just so he can deliver tax cuts to billionaires,” and called on him to refund donations from Jeffrey Epstein–linked billionaires. She swore off “corporate PAC money” and pledged to “rein in the influence of corporations and billionaires in our elections.” When Graham died and was replaced by his sister, Darline, Andrews hammered her for the same thing. Andrews called her “handpicked and bought by big corporations,” attacked her for doing the bidding of a data center industry spending millions of dollars of dark money to get her elected, and pointed to the $27 million that “outside Super PACs” had spent to support her. She won by nearly 5 points. This was a very different campaign than the one former corporate lobbyist Jaime Harrison ran against Lindsey Graham six years ago. Since Harrison was relying on corporate bundlers and billionaire donors to raise obscene amounts of money to outspend Graham, he couldn’t and didn’t launch any of these attacks — in fact, Graham turned it around on him, complaining that outside dark money was flooding in to support the Democrat. Harrison’s attacks on Graham were focused on the idea that voters couldn’t trust him, because he had gone back on his word in supporting Donald Trump’s 2020 Supreme Court pick. He lost by 10 points. Senator-elect Annie Andrews pledged to “rein in the influence of corporations and billionaires in our elections.” (York County Democratic Party / CC BY 4.0 ) Or look at Josh Turek, who won Iowa by four points against GOP candidate Ashley Hinson. Turek constantly talked about how Washington was full of millionaires “looking out for billionaires” and that he was “not one of them,” nor did he take corporate PAC money or was “owned by billionaires” (even as he quietly did take money from some billionaires). Iowa’s Republican senators and, he implied , his opponent , were “just looking out for billionaires and large corporations.” During a debate , in attack ads , and in a Des Moines Register op-ed , Turek took aim at Hinson’s personal wealth, complaining that she had “gotten richer in her time in Washington” while slashing social spending on working-class Iowans, slamming her for her stock ownership, and saying that “we have a corruption crisis that’s leading to an affordability crisis because we’re sending people like Ashley Hinson up to DC” to line their pockets. Not even Sanders went this hard against his wealthy opponents. Then look at Michael Franken’s campaign for an Iowa Senate seat four years earlier. Though Franken prominently swore off corporate PAC donations, there was no talk of billionaires or wealth inequality. Franken appealed to “that middle segment who want logical, pragmatic, smart, dedicated, national servants to work for them,” and ran on a message that “we need to put country over party” and “people over politics.” He jabbed at his opponent’s age and long tenure in office, framed himself as defending democracy and minority rights, particularly those of women, whose right to an abortion he frequently brought up. And he ended up losing by 12 points. Over in Mississippi, where prosecutor Scott Colom eked out a shock win to become the state’s first black senator, he did it by similarly assailing his Republican opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s donations from “millionaires and billionaires” out of state and accusing her of throwing tens of thousands of Mississippians off their health insurance “to look out for people in California and New York,” specifically “billionaires and millionaires” there, by giving them a “ billionaire tax break .” He ran on raising taxes on the rich and getting rid of corporate subsidies for billionaires, and hit his opponent for staying silent on data centers being pushed by “AI billionaires” while being backed by a pro-AI super PAC. This did not happen two years earlier, when Ty Pinkins (who ran, to some controversy, as a third-party candidate this year) ran for the other Mississippi US Senate seat, once again eschewing any kind of bold economic message in favor of warning that “our very democracy is being threatened” by people attacking its “institutional safeguards,” in his announcement . Pinkins said his platform revolved around the vague motto of, “You talk, I listen, we do,” which he explained (in even vaguer terms) meant, “I can listen and hear what’s important to their communities,” and then “do what’s necessary to move these communities and our state forward.” That campaign lost by nearly 30 points. A particularly instructive example is Sherrod Brown in Ohio, who lost reelection to his Senate seat by nearly 4 points in 2024, then won the other Senate seat this year by just under 5 points. Despite a long-standing and deserved reputation as a populist, Brown said very little about millionaires and billionaires two years ago, other than that they should “ pay their fair share ” into Social Security — even as they were spending massive amounts to defeat him, which they did. Sherrod Brown boasted that “From Elon Musk to Donald Trump, billionaires are spending hundreds of millions of dollars against me.” (Marc Nozell / CC BY 2.0 ) In 2026, more or less the official motto of Brown’s campaign was “Workers Before Billionaires,” a phrase he put in press releases , merchandise , tweets , Substack posts , reels , TikToks , and video after video . Compare his demure response two years earlier to a question about Republicans backing personally wealthy candidates — “That’s who they are . . . I guess I’m not surprised by that” — to what he said about his 2026 GOP opponent, Jon Husted: “The disdain, the contempt they have for work and for workers tells you everything.” This time Brown, who called for a tax hike on billionaires, went in on Husted’s connection to the ultrarich and what the campaign characterized as his “ corruption ”: “Clevelanders have seen time and time again how Husted bows down to billionaires and corporations while leaving hardworking Ohioans behind.” ( August 29 ) “Jon Husted’s for sale and the billionaires and corporations pouring millions into this race know it.” ( September 21 ) “Ohioans have watched Jon Husted put billionaires and corporations before working families time and time again.” ( October 3 ) “From Elon Musk to Donald Trump, billionaires are spending hundreds of millions of dollars against me because they know they can buy Jon Husted’s votes.” ( October 29 ) For good measure, Brown ran at least three separate TV ads hitting Husted for taking more money from Les Wexner, the disgraced Epstein-connected Ohio billionaire, than anyone else in Congress. It is hard to make the case that nothing has changed when the same candidate ran a completely different campaign just two years later. Finally, take a look at North Carolina, home to the second largest US financial center after New York, and where former governor Roy Cooper beat the Republican candidate by nearly 20 points. “Time to elect a senator for everyday people, not billionaires,” Cooper said after winning the primary, a theme he came back to over and over again, whether saying that “we don’t have the billionaires they do,” that his opponent was “fighting for the billionaire friends he made while working as a Big Oil and utility company lobbyist in DC,” or hitting Trump’s bill “that gave tax cuts to billionaires” and had “driven healthcare premiums up.” Senator-elect Cooper charged his opponent with “fighting for the billionaire friends he made while working as a Big Oil and utility company lobbyist in DC.” (North Carolina Department of Communications / CC BY 2.0 ) Again, Cooper has a well-established reputation as a moderate, but this kind of rhetoric simply bore no resemblance to the Senate campaign run by another moderate, former state Supreme Court Chief Justice Cheri Beasley in 2022. Beasley centered her campaign on abortion rights and health care generally, and talked about diversity and reforming the criminal justice system to fix the “disparities” that exist within it while touting her support from law enforcement. There was no talk of billionaires or dark money, since Beasley herself was backed by twenty-three billionaires and won her primary by being boosted by various out-of-state PACs. She lost by 3 points. This is borne out by research by Eric Blanc. Going through candidate websites in 2024 and 2026, he found that while billionaires were referenced in only 19 percent of candidates’ websites two years ago, this year they featured in 78 percent. Meanwhile, research by the Center for Working Class Politics found that less than 20 percent of the candidates in 2024 attacked corporations, billionaires, or Wall Street for their role in the affordability crisis. Admitting Defeat in Victory The fact that these candidates used populist rhetoric doesn’t necessarily mean they are populists, or even progressive. A number of these candidates have taken money from the billionaires they decry, including Talarico, and did not necessarily run on very ambitious policies. Meanwhile, Cooper is a multimillionaire himself, and like several others, did not run on taxing the rich, for all the class-war-style rhetoric that was thrown around. But it does mean that Democratic moderates have tacitly accepted what voices on the Left have been saying for years, which is that the Bernie Sanders pitch — of a corrupt, rigged system pitting billionaires and corporations against working Americans — has broad appeal that cuts across geographic, racial, and, yes, sometimes even partisan lines. Whatever they may tell you now, centrists did not always feel this way. Third Way cofounder Matt Bennett, for instance, was one of the corporate centrists insisting that there was nothing remarkable about any of this, because Sanders was not “the first Democratic (adjacent) candidate to use populist rhetoric in the modern era.” This will be news to Third Way circa 2016, whose president celebrated Sanders’s loss in the Democratic primary that year, because if “liberal populism doesn’t win Democratic primaries,” then it can’t “be the path back for a party” in a general election, and showed that “voters are angry, but they don’t want to focus mainly on billionaires.” Likewise, Matthew Yglesias today may mock clueless young people thinking “Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes.” But back in 2016, he listed Sanders’s plans to “soak the rich to a much greater extent” as one of the supposedly risky, radical ideas that made “the vast majority of the party’s elected officials and interest group leaders” worry about him. Stances like that were “not popular,” Yglesias wrote, and made him unelectable, compared to Hillary Clinton’s “relatively modest, overwhelmingly popular tweaks to the tax code.” Something interesting is happening here. For years, frustrated socialists and progressives have been arguing that opposition to billionaires, soaking the ultrarich, and getting money out of politics are the centrist positions: that Americans across all walks of life — white or black, college-educated or not, liberal or conservative, in blue, red, or purple states — were pretty united on this, regardless of their exact views on things like immigration, guns, or trans kids in sports. Whatever the pundits are saying, centrist candidates seem to have finally acknowledged that’s the case.
