articles.title: Five Things Socialists In Congress Should Do
articles.author: Will S.
articles.content: Congress is about to boast more socialists than ever before. DSA seems poised to double or triple our Congressional slate in 2028 and 2030, but we actually say very little about what our federal representatives are supposed to do with their positions. Most of the discussion around our Socialists in Office, at all levels, is about passing legislation, but we need to acknowledge that right now we don’t even have the numbers or the organization to stop the priorities of our enemies in both parties, like tax cuts or more oil drilling, let alone to enact Medicare for All. We of course want to win non-reformist reforms to weaken capital and boost workers’ ability to fight. But to get there, we’ll need to go through a phase of growth, experimentation, and probably getting our asses kicked a bit. Getting through – and getting the most out of – this phase is complicated even more by the fact that we live in the age of lobbyism. Most legislation in this country is passed exclusively through backroom deals. When we talk about lobbyists, most people think of AIPAC, conservative think tanks, tech giants, or crypto, but lobbying is also the primary method of doing politics for our progressive allies like NGOs and establishment-friendly union leaders. This means, unfortunately, that some of our candidates’ backgrounds are just in this kind of obscure political work. Nowhere is lobbyism more concentrated and more rancid than in Congress. We believe that mass action by millions of working-class people organizing together, not handshakes in smoke-filled rooms, is the right path for the democratic road to socialism. We don’t think socialism can be enacted from above. A different theory of change requires a different mode of politics, not a better business as usual. To demonstrate this mass action politics, our politicians – particularly our Federal Socialists in Office – need to build the socialist movement: agitate for our demands and grow our base by involving more working-class people in political struggle. Here are five things that Federal Socialists can do: 1. Stick Together The quickest way to get crushed as a Socialist in Office (SIO) is to try to go it alone. Our SIOs are constantly inundated by proponents of lobbyism, which would mean spending less and less time with working-class people or socialist cadre. Each socialist elected who gets picked off by establishment Democrats will weaken these connections further until they’re isolated from the movements and organizers who gave them their office. No base, no mass movement. The best antidote is to stick together with fellow FSIOs in a Socialist Caucus. Caucusing together will let us move in unison, develop clear political lines so we don’t have to approach each crisis from square one, and help DSA become even more party-like. This means that when a DSA member runs for Congress, all our Socialist Caucus members of the House endorse that candidate, and the candidate uses our lists to fundraise and phonebank. We’ll have to combine the capacity of our comrades’ offices, their bases of support, and DSA both locally and nationally to compete with the lobbyists’ money and influence. 2. Make Enemies When a comrade occupies an elected office, they’re organizing in a parallel reality to the vast majority of people in the world. This new reality can be politically disorienting, which suits the lobbyists just fine. But allies outside won’t understand the daily reality of navigating the halls of power, which can start a vicious cycle of distrust and miscommunication within movements. In order to survive the lobbyists’ world, our Socialist Caucus should make our hatred of them clear; that goes doubly for our socialists’ “colleagues” who attack us on behalf of their donors. When lobbyists come for them, we should respond publicly. When billionaire-bought politicians come for them, we should tell everyone. We should take pride in naming our enemies. It’s good not to get invited to the Christmas party when the party is made up of weapons manufacturers and pedophiles! Our mass politics are a threat to the lobbyists’ careers. They will tell us that we won’t get anywhere by alienating them. They’ll try to block our priorities, spend millions supporting our opponents, and try to poison the bonds between us and our constituents. We can’t control everything our enemies do, and they’re weaker than we know. We can only double down on mass action and build our movement until the lobbyists are marginalized. JP Lyninger was elected to the Louisville, Kentucky, city council in late 2024. He says, “When anyone takes office, they’re swarmed by people who are asking if you can be bought, bullied, or used, or some combination of the three. Whether the lobbyists represent business interests or nonprofit coalitions looking for financial and policy support, they’re professionals whose job is to steer the agenda of government. “Being transparent about these interactions and working with my chapter, Louisville DSA, to take these power dynamics out from behind closed doors and into public awareness is vital for our organizing and for the long-term political education of the working class. If we aren’t arming working people with this knowledge, how can they be political protagonists?” 3. Touch Grass It’s something of a joke in American politics how much time Congresspeople spend in Washington and how little they return to their home districts. But we’re doing mass action, which means constantly going back home to uplift the working-class people of our FSIOs’ districts. We can hold town halls on widely and deeply felt issues attached to our Socialist Caucus’s program, join local movement efforts that connect with DSA’s national campaigns, and use our combined lists and influence to grow the movement outside of Washington. We’re in a moment where we’re massively expanding the “supporter” ring of our movement’s “bullseye,” but we should make no mistake: an electorate is not a base. As Eugene Debs put it, “Voting for socialism is not socialism any more than a menu is a meal.” We need to focus on moving new supporters into the activist ring by plugging them into concrete organizing asks and local DSA chapters. We should seek funding in national budgets for projects that can build our base back home, especially when they’re tied to the demands of socialists and social movements. The Belgian Workers’ Party took state money and built party health clinics in order to organize a base of support. Our FSIOs should also campaign for socialist candidates in their home districts who emerge from DSA and social movements. 4. Put Our Issues on the Table Right now, socialists are an extreme minority in Congress, meaning we don’t have much hope of immediately passing the non-reformist reforms we need to weaken capital and grow the working class’s ability to fight. That doesn’t mean we can’t have a big impact on the U.S. political landscape and discourse — we can still put issues on the table. Even if we don’t think a bill can pass, the Socialist Caucus should introduce legislation that majorities of Americans support and use these moments as an educational and organizing opportunity. Long-shot bills like Bernie’s Medicare for All Act or the Block the Bombs Act give something tangible for social movements to organize around and let us challenge other electeds to sign on. If they refuse, we can use their refusal to run socialists against them next cycle. Even when a bill doesn’t pass, it helps us gauge the strength of our movement and our capacity for public pressure. It also lets us direct the media towards our demands and away from whatever bullshit the corporate parties want working people focused on instead. 5. Make a Scene Our FSIOs are some of the most highly visible members of our movement. That visibility means they can help our message reach beyond our normal activist base into the broader working class. Likewise, they more than anyone will help shape the public’s conception of socialism. If they don’t define socialism for millions of Americans, our enemies will. The best way to use the bully pulpit is to get in the news constantly in a way that can’t be ignored. Think AOC occupying Nancy Pelosi’s office along with the Sunrise Movement, Rashida’s sign during Netanyahu’s speech, and Bernie’s legendary filibuster . The Socialist Caucus should write a good stump speech for socialism, making it clear that we’re not just referring to libraries and fire protection, and have our members give it at every single opportunity. We should clip speeches and actions and share them on social media. Our FSIOs should be in constant communication with the public; former Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s’s daily morning press conferences and Zohran’s slew of short-form videos are good examples. Our electeds should make video interviews with working-class people in their districts, showing the realities of their daily lives and how our platform can change their lives for the better. Entering a government made by and for capitalists is one of the toughest things we can ask a comrade to do. When we stick together, we can resist the siren song of lobbyism (and have a good time doing it). The post Five Things Socialists In Congress Should Do appeared first on The Call .

articles.title: Beyond Trump
articles.author: Richard Wolff
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The mid-term elections can teach us much more than that the Trumpian brand of Republican Party is out of tune with most Americans or that billionaires’ donations can turn voters off or even that both parties’ support of Israel has been sharply reduced. The vote was more against the Republicans than it was for the Democrats. The key lesson for Democrats to learn is the danger they face if they revert to the cozy pre-2026 decades of alternating Republican and Democratic presidents and congresses. Those had presided over a changing US capitalism in a changing world. The post-1945 American empire had enriched very few. They used that wealth to buy US politics. And they used a bought politics to roll back the New Deal won by US workers out of the ruins of the 1930s Great Depression. Together, the super-rich and their bought politicians took back the jobs, incomes, plans and dreams won in that New Deal. The Republicans did that quickly, while the Democrats slowed it down. Neither party fought to build on what the New Deal has begun. If the post-2026 Democratic Party reverts to what it was under Clinton, Obama, Biden, and Harris, it will invite an electoral shellacking as bad as what just hit Trump’s Republicans. After all, Trump had promised to end the forever wars, to reshore manufacturing back to the US, to stop and undo inflation, to address the long-deepening US inequalities of wealth and income (chiefly by mass deportation of the poorest), and to achieve a lost “greatness.” He accomplished none of these goals. He aggravated many of them. But he always took credit for solving every one of them. Trumpers even scolded the mass of Americans for not giving him and his closest associates that credit for those non-existent accomplishments. Meanwhile, only the rich got richer (and the super-rich even richer still) as we were all reminded over and over. That’s why we all remember that famous image when an elated Elon Musk – capitalism’s first trillionaire - wielded a chain-saw symbolizing his cutting of hundreds of thousands of federal jobs (gutting the public services they had provided). By November, 2026, this record proved way too much for millions of voters. Their hope for change had itself changed to anger and disgust at the sheer scale of what Trump had failed to deliver. Related: China and the US: Meeting Is Good, Agreement Is Better Most of the most progressive candidates did very well and that sends an additional message to the Democratic Party. To avoid repeating the Trump disaster, that Party better offer and fight hard for more and far bigger real changes than it traditionally has. Taxes on the incomes and wealth of the rich and super-rich must finally be raised to what they were in the 1960s. National rent controls and the building of quality public housing are long overdue. Jobs must be guaranteed for those unemployed now and for those subject to unemployment if and when AI enriches its billionaire boosters. Pensions must be guaranteed for all working Americans: both those now on social security and those who arrive in the future. Changing the burden of taxation, ending the forever wars, and refusing to start new ones can free funds needed to accomplish big changes. And if Trump repeatedly vetoes Democrats’ honest efforts for big changes, ejecting Trump Republicans from the presidency in 2028 becomes the Democratic campaign. Here is a sample of the types of domestic changes Democrats need to undertake: an explicit commitment to US income redistribution to approximate that of the 1960s and parallel wealth redistribution; national rent control plus pubic housing construction program; development of a cooperative enterprise sector of the US economy to compete with the capitalist sector; a broad jobs program for today’s unemployed and those who become unemployed if and when AI takes their jobs; a moratorium of AI investment until a government plan is adopted to manage its disruption of the economy; a raised national minimum and a reasonably maximum wage established and enforced; and a serious commitment to reverse the rules allowing money to flow into and buy our politics. Here is a sample of the types of foreign policy changes Democrats need to undertake: propose to meet with Chinese leaders to chart a shared course for peaceful economic development of both sides (instead of military posturing); propose to host tri-lateral meeting of Europe, Russia, and US aimed to agree on a new security architecture for Europe; coordinate ends to wars in Iran, Israel, and Ukraine as a global joint priority and responsibility; normalize diplomatic and economic relationships with Cuba, Venezuela and all other nations. Related: From Welfare State to Warfare State: Europe’s Dangerous Turn These are dramatic breakthroughs away from what has become a stale, old failed political program of traditional Republicans and Democrats. Such breakthroughs are what the world needs and millions of Americans are more ready to support than ever before. The question is whether the Democrats can find and nurture effective leadership that dares to think big and act bigger. For these directions are the only ones available to snatch greatness from the jaws of a relentlessly declining American empire. Nothing offers the American labor movement the chance to regain its position of inspiring and leading mass movements for progressive change – what it did so dramatically and effectively in the 1930s – than stepping up here and now. Who else in American society right now could gather all the social movements to such an end? The actual government we get does not depend on what the parties do. It depends on what the people make or allow their parties, old and new, to do.

articles.title: Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
articles.author: Kap Seol
articles.content: Possible Love is yet another masterpiece that South Korean director Lee Chang-dong has brought to us, after an eight-year hiatus since his last film Burning (2018). Unlike his younger Korean peers, such as Bong Joon-ho ( Parasite ) or Park Chan-wook ( Old Boy and No Other Choice ), Lee, now seventy-two, has often found himself confined to the independent film scene outside South Korea, where he has usually enjoyed modest commercial success. Deeply rooted in humanity and class relations, Lee’s films deserve a wider audience beyond the ranks of art house aficionados (including Barack Obama, who named Burning among his favorite movies of 2018). Lee’s 1999 film Peppermint Candy weaves the life of a young man into the breakneck pace of South Korean capitalism, showing how innocence loses ground to violence, avarice, and lust. Burning explores the ways in which capitalism preys on and consumes poor young men and women. Netflix’s funding and global distribution of Possible Love will likely expand Lee’s global reach. However, it has also revealed the maestro’s inability to raise further funds in South Korea, whose media giants — mostly outgrowths of chaebol conglomerates such as CJ ENM or Lotte Entertainment — no longer appear to be willing to bankroll Lee’s bold and unapologetic portrayal of South Korea’s economic system. The Living and the Dead For Netflix, Possible Love is a prestige project: an opportunity to bring home an Oscar with a highly accomplished director while reversing a viewership slump and enhancing its brand. Possible Love premiered theatrically in South Korea in September, meeting the Academy’s country-of-origin eligibility deadline . The streaming platform has also made Lee’s previous films available for its subscribers. Possible Love is set against the aftermath of the 2009 brutal crackdown on the seventy-seven-day strike against massive job cuts at SsangYong Motor (fictionalized in the film as SP Heavy Industries). After crushing the strike, management and the government pushed through one of the country’s first massive layoffs by slashing 50 percent of SsangYong’s blue-collar workforce. In the film as in real life, workers refer to their laid-off colleagues as “the dead” and those who managed to escape the cull as “the living.” Through the crackdown, corporations and the conservative government set a precedent for mass layoffs. After the defeat at SsangYong, corporations could cut jobs by invoking broadly defined criteria of managerial exigency. The repercussions of the strike and its vivid suppression resonated deeply throughout South Korea. The strike even became part of the backstory of Squid Game , Netflix’s gamified portrayal of capitalist suffering. In his review of the series, Lee Chang-kun, a leader of SsangYong’s labor union, summed up the experience of an agonizing and prolonged factory occupation: Out of the blue, we were left with no option but to squat at the factory. We first attempted to turn to each other to survive together. However, we were thrown into a life-or-death situation, often with no other option but to betray and dupe each other. At least once, as in Squid Game , we each had to hurt our closest friends. Many workers or their family members have since died by suicide or from stress-related conditions such as cardiac arrest. There was probably no better place for Lee to begin Possible Love than the funeral of one such worker. Anger and Betrayal In the film, Ho-seok (played by Peppermint Candy star Sul Kyung-gu) was one of the remaining seven hundred striking workers who faced the violent police raid. He had been a welder, proud enough to name his son “Iron.” Having been injured in the crackdown and subsequently jailed, he has been drained of his blue-collar mettle and sense of purpose, leaving him with simmering feelings of anger and betrayal. His wife, Mi-ok ( Secret Sunshine star Jeon Do-yeon) is a good-hearted, innately resilient former seamstress who does her best to hold the family together against all odds in the wake of her husband’s layoff. At this point, documentary director Ye-ji — played by Cho Yeo-jeong, almost typecast as the seemingly innocuous upper-class woman after her similar role in Parasite — encroaches on Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s fragile universe with her camera lens. A daughter of a small-business owner turned parvenu, Ye-ji is married to Sang-woo ( Hope star Zo In-sung), a private equity investor born into generations of wealth and power. Ye-ji attempts to love Mi-ok and Ho-seok because she believes herself to be a good person. While she is probably sympathetic to Ho-seok and his family, she is strikingly lacking in empathy for their situation. Her superficial innocuousness is pernicious. Ye-ji’s interest in laid-off workers from SP Industries began during a vacation at a resort in the middle of the Qatar desert, maintained by workers who, her husband tells her, labored hard behind the scenes. Ho-seok is a subject Ye-ji wants to capture through her camera before he disappears into obscurity. Ye-ji’s husband, Sang-woo, is kind and well-mannered, probably because he has little reason to be otherwise. In his line of business, everything seems impersonal, reduced to numbers and valuations. Although he possesses greater worldly insight than his wife, he need not concern himself with the consequences of his spreadsheets for people like Ho-seok, who remain invisible to him. There seems to be nothing Ho-seok can do better than Sang-woo. The latter is the better husband, always supportive of his wife, both morally and financially. He is also the better athlete, having tutored the welder’s son in tae kwon do, the sport in which Ho-seok was once a varsity athlete. To add insult to injury, he is even a superior musician who can play the oboe while Mi-ok sings at karaoke. Ho-seok keeps his guard up around Sang-woo, but he seems to be free of personal jealousy toward him, as though he instinctively feels that the rift between them is one of class rather than individual attributes. Rather, what has traumatized Ho-seok is the experience of his coworkers, who are now divided into the living and the dead. He has feelings of envy toward the living; they can still throw a fancy birthday party for their children. Emotionally overwhelmed, Ho-seok cannot open up during a group therapy session, where one of the dead laments that they were defeated despite being on the right side. Impossible Love It is painful to watch Ho-seok, especially if you understand how strikes and campaigns are defeated — how they implode before they can fizzle out or are violently crushed. We do not walk away from our collective struggles because we abruptly come to fear or love our adversaries. We walk away because we have grown disillusioned or lost trust in the people beside us. It is before Ye-ji’s camera that Ho-seok finally breaks down in tears and confesses his deepest fear that his wife and former coworkers will discover the anger and sense of betrayal he has kept deep inside. Words like “solidarity” or “resistance” have been reduced to hollow shells of what they used to mean to him. It is also when Ye-ji finally lowers her intrusive camera, perhaps stunned by the scene, or perhaps realizing she can never genuinely understand (or love) her subjects. Her very innocuity is a form of violence against Ho-seok and Mi-ok. “That’s enough!” both Ye-ji and Mi-ok yell after Ho-seok’s moment opening-up. The two couples part ways. Director Lee appears to have built the narrative around one of the Ten Commandments, “You shall not covet,” which appears at the beginning of the film. Ye-ji has even coveted Ho-seok’s agonies. For Ho-seok, that suffering still constitutes part of his own dignity. After opening up, he appears to regain part of his strength. When Mi-ok asks for the first time in the film about their future, “What shall we do?” he answers, “We will keep living on.” “It will rain tomorrow,” his wife says. “It hasn’t today,” her husband replies, as if that were how he has put himself together day by day since the strike was crushed. Possible Love is difficult to watch because it relentlessly makes you uncomfortable, if not downright pained. Ho-seok is not an idealized figure: he is a wavering worker, trapped in divisions within his own class, rather than a bold and brave militant taking on his boss and the system. However, this makes his character all the more real: like Ho-seok and the film itself, we are all multilayered beings defying any simple definition. articles.title: US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
articles.author: Kelly McKowen
articles.content: For several years, I lived in Norway and enjoyed the privileges associated with membership in Folketrygden , or the National Insurance Scheme. One privilege that I still think about often is the relative frictionlessness of interacting with the Norwegian government. Seeing a doctor, for example, was effortless, and once my low annual deductible (as of 2026, ~$300) was paid, all testing and treatment for the year was covered without my involvement or input. My taxes were — without my prompting — prepared for me and sent for my amendment and approval. There was never anything to amend, of course. And because of the country’s leveringsfritak , or “silent acceptance” law, I did not even have to sign or submit a return. The great difference between how things are typically done in Norway and how they are done in my home country, the United States, was never clearer to me than it was one day when I had to visit the US embassy in Oslo to handle some paperwork. At that time, the embassy was housed in an angular, charcoal-colored Eero Saarinen building across the street from the Royal Palace. It was not only conveniently located but, despite its popular reputation as a “fortress,” simple and straightforward to access — entering the compound required flashing my passport and was about as easy as doing anything else in Norway. Imagine my surprise, then, when I arrived at the office where I was to complete my task: from the uncomfortable seating and oppressive lighting to the interminable wait and general feeling of disaffection, it was such an uncanny recreation of an underfunded Department of Motor Vehicles or post office that it could have been a movie set. There was even a small, cheaply framed photo of the president. The juxtaposition of this experience — which seemed designed to frustrate — and my happy dealings with Norway’s bureaucracies was, in its own way, radicalizing. I sense that Annie Lowrey, author of The Time Tax , has been similarly radicalized, albeit through extensive personal and journalistic exposure to the myriad forms in which people in the United States have their time wasted and disrespected — or “taxed,” as she puts it — in almost every conceivable interaction with the government. She is clearly and justifiably pissed, and her book endeavors to show that the problem is, though widespread and deeply rooted in a particular national history of racial exclusion and class oppression, fixable. There is a world, she argues, beyond our current patchwork of fool’s errands and wild-goose chases. The Time Tax and Its Origins But it is to this patchwork — and its associated “time taxes” — that most of the book is devoted. Through a mix of reporting, social scientific research, and reflecting on her own experience with an autoimmune condition, Lowrey has collected a cabinet of maddening curiosities: impenetrable forms, inexplicable rejections, multiyear wait times, and more. Page after page finds ordinary Americans trying to navigate a twisted institutional terrain seemingly designed by Franz Kafka or M. C. Escher. In the United States, you can buy, bid, and bet with the click of a button. Yet paying your taxes, voting, and getting benefits for which you qualify requires you to do American Ninja Warrior — with the proper forms of ID in hand. Having cataloged the challenges people face when using public services in the United States, the first section of The Time Tax concludes with a tantalizing glimpse at the Estonian case, which, in many ways, resembles the Norwegian one with which I am more familiar (sans generous welfare state and strong labor rights). The story, as told by Lowrey, is that the small Baltic country, battered and bereft after exiting the Soviet Union, lacked the time, experience, infrastructure, and resources to recreate the comprehensive service architectures of other countries. So it didn’t. Instead, a generation of young and enterprising leaders leaned into speed, convenience, and digital integration to build an innovative e-government. In Estonia, Lowrey has seen the almost frictionless future of navigating government — and it works! The Time Tax is at its most interesting and convincing when Lowrey is detailing the diabolical busy boxes that occupy millions of Americans. After the brief field trip to Estonia, the book could — and probably should — have ended with her proposals. It doesn’t. Perhaps drawing inspiration from her subject, Lowrey decides that she requires more of her reader’s time to make her point. After a section break, we leave Estonia and arrive at . . . Fort Pillow in 1864? With Confederate general and future Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard Nathan Bedford Forrest? It was disappointing to discover that The Time Tax was not in fact beginning its descent to a satisfying landing — it had been diverted to another destination: the past. The middle third of the book draws on the extensive historical and social scientific scholarship devoted to the United States’ welfare system to recapitulate a story that will be familiar to anyone who knows the tortuous history of social provision in the United States. All the beats are there: Civil War pensions, Jim Crow, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and the Great Depression, Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society, Ronald Reagan’s “welfare queens,” Bill Clinton and the “end of welfare as we know it.” Lowrey provides some useful context for twenty-first-century annoyances but breaks no new ground here, and the long historical detour saps the momentum of her opening chapters. I worry that it also leads her to draw the wrong conclusions about her time taxes. She laments, for instance, that “diversity creates time taxes” and suggests that we are not Estonia due to “racial makeup.” Could it not be instead that time taxes transform diversity into inequality and hierarchy? Cutting the Time Tax? In any case, the final part of the book picks up the threads of the first to make a final appeal and offer Lowrey’s solutions. This appeal takes for granted that the reader has not been entirely swayed by their own experiences or by the book’s emphasis on aggravation, injustice, racism, and inequality. Instead, Lowrey makes a persuasive closing argument that time taxes also hurt our health, teach us the wrong lessons about citizenship and government, and undermine social trust. She concludes with her blueprint for change. Her proposed fixes include measuring time taxes via “sludge audits,” federalizing what are today state-run programs, reducing the use of means-testing in favor of universalism, and abolishing work requirements and pro forma interviews. These changes would, in the aggregate, make using public services faster, easier, more convenient, more empowering, and ultimately more fulfilling. But I hesitate to call these proposals “solutions,” because I do not think that they actually address the problem at the heart of The Time Tax . This problem is not time taxes per se but the success of actors who weaponize bureaucracy to undermine our access to the goods and services of the social citizenship for which previous generations have fought and even died. The status quo in the United States is a nightmare not because elites are unaware of the fact that universalism promotes greater public investment and trust in government — it is a nightmare because they are aware. The history of many hitherto existing time taxes is also the history of class struggles. Lowrey knows this — I think. She condemns TurboTax for helping to kill Direct File, Florida Republicans for fighting the reenfranchisement of convicted felons, and Donald Trump for the disaster of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)–related cuts. She tells us that “time taxes are not just policy failures, but deliberate tools of social control.” And yet The Time Tax ’s antagonist is without question “Uncle Sam” (her chosen shorthand for the government) and his “bureaucratic excesses.” The issue is that while she lambasts “Uncle Sam” again and again, she is hesitant to center the private interests for whom that control is useful and profitable. In her long historical excursus, she can acknowledge that poll taxes and other discriminatory laws were used by racist white elites to exclude black people, make their lives precarious, and destroy governmental alternatives to foster dependency on actors who rarely had their best interests in mind. But while the past has opponents, for Lowrey, the present only has design flaws. A smaller rhetorical point: Lowrey undermines her cause with the book’s core metaphor. Calling the problem the “time tax” might sell books to tax-wary Americans, but it could reinforce the pernicious idea that taxes do not benefit ordinary people. This is odd, as Lowrey herself acknowledges that a sustainable remedy to “the headaches, snafus, and frustration imposed by Uncle Sam” requires the expansion and improvement of administrative capacity — a development that would almost certainly require, well, greater taxes. Finally, there is a problem of conceptual imprecision, which becomes apparent in the book’s first pages. Lowrey opens The Time Tax with a montage, juxtaposing disconnected scenarios for the purpose of creating a connective thread — the time tax — between radically different people, places, and challenges. But as she moves from losing the right to vote, to trying to get insurance to cover therapies for an autistic child, to attempting to open a soft-serve ice cream shop, to practicing cosmetology without a license, to handing out burritos to the homeless without a permit, I began to question whether each of these is in fact an example of the same problem. After a while, she more or less abandons any attempt to persuade you that a given obstacle is or is not a time tax. Instead, she just asserts it, identifying one or more annoyances and then adding something like “ — a time tax,” as if it were obvious. All in all, The Time Tax is laudable as a collection of curios. It is less useful as a blueprint. Though Lowrey knows — and sometimes says explicitly — that this maddening status quo reflects the desires of certain powerful and well-resourced actors, she offers no proposals for organizing to muzzle, defang, or otherwise diminish their influence. She writes that “change does not happen without awareness, and awareness is not possible without numbers and stories.” But it also does not happen without an awareness of who or what benefits from keeping you trapped in a thousand purgatories and a strategy for organizing against them. The path to a Norwegian-style welfare state is not just a matter of design — it is one of politics, and class politics in particular. articles.title: Like Benjamin Franklin
articles.author: Dimitris Eleas
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Some people make history when they win the presidency; others, like Benjamin Franklin, shaped the nation without ever holding its highest office. Americans have voted on the six years of Donald Trump's era of excess. Four years of his first presidency and two of his second. The November 3 midterm elections offered a glimmer of hope for American democracy. The big question was whether the Democrats would manage to regain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, putting a check on the president. They succeeded in both chambers ! The results send a message of change. They marked the end of the political careers of many politicians. Trump governed, and continues to govern, with a personal, often imperial style, one eyebrow raised and a glint in his eye, often treating the presidency as if it were his private business. His political presence, somewhere between the excesses of a Hollywood star and the behavior of a Wild West saloon owner, has created deep divisions within society. Under his leadership, America has often looked like a Wild West movie set. But democracy is no one’s spoils. Related: The AI Race Is Accelerating: Who Will Hit the Brakes? The most important issue is people’s everyday lives. The high cost of food, the cost of energy and housing, the uncertainty surrounding healthcare, and ICE’s harsh immigration operations have created an explosive social environment. Thousands of families are living in fear of deportation. The slogan “America First” has devolved into “America First for the Few” – an America that puts the financially powerful and billionaires first. And so, Elon Musk backed the Republicans with $446 million , only to see that money go up in smoke. However, the Republican Party is not the only one responsible for what is happening in America today. The Democrats also bear a significant share of the responsibility. For three decades, to a large extent, they forgot the poor and the working class. They moved away from the real concerns of society and left room for Trump’s populism. You cannot defend democracy if you are indifferent to social justice. I am 100% politically independent. Today, however, I believe that America needs a strong opposition, and fortunately, it will have one. It needs new politicians with social sensitivity, but also the political vision of someone like Senator Bernie Sanders. If he had been given the opportunity to run for president and win in 2016, perhaps America today would be different. Related: Trump Suspends Attack on Iran but Who are the Real Winners and Losers Of course, a politician’s historical importance is not measured by whether he becomes president, but by the ideas he leaves behind and the changes he inspires. Benjamin Franklin never became president, yet secured a permanent place in American history. Perhaps Sanders, in his own way, will do the same. (Actually, many people think Mr. $100 Bill was indeed a president!) He lost the nomination back then because the Democratic Party undermined him in favor of the warmongering Hillary Clinton. The Democratic Party must start talking again about decent wages, public healthcare, and tax fairness. Bernie advocates for Medicare for All and a nationwide minimum wage of $20 an hour. And the party must use even the word socialism wisely, a word that continues to make a large part of American society uncomfortable. The Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and Trump will now face a strong institutional counterweight. He will no longer be able to treat Congress as a mechanism for automatically approving his decisions. But this victory is not a blank check. It requires responsibility, unity, and political maturity on the part of the Democrats. Related: Why Iran War Is Not Going Well for U.S. and Israel We are living through historic moments. America’s Founders, Franklin among them, created institutions precisely to protect democracy from the excessive concentration of power or the emergence of the kind of phenomena we have witnessed over these six years. Today, the Democrats, above all, are called upon to defend them in practice. It is a great country, with weaknesses, contradictions, and enormous potential. The scale of the Republicans’ stunning defeat , however, may, in time, also help heal the wounds left behind by the Trump hurricane as it swept through politics and society. Perhaps the cracks already present within the MAGA movement’s base will grow even wider. But the Party of Reagan, too, will have to wake up from its deep slumber. Even Mitt Romney has called for a “ course correction ” within his party. And some of the political seeds Bernie Sanders planted have finally borne fruit. Several candidates he endorsed won their races, giving the progressive movement a stronger voice in Congress. Sanders’s lasting legacy is his vision of a society for all and a government for the many, not just the few. Electoral victories may be short-lived, but the power of ideas is eternal. Personality is what makes a human being a history-making creature! Franklin left his mark without becoming president. Sanders has achieved something similar in our time. And who knows? If America one day introduces a $200 bill, the Wise and Independent Man of Vermont may appear on it. He would certainly deserve it.

articles.title: Eugene Debs’s Life Speaks to Today’s Socialist Movement
articles.author: Nelson Lichtenstein
articles.content: Shawn Gude’s splendid new biography of Gilded Age Socialist Eugene V. Debs could hardly have arrived at a more propitious moment. Perhaps as many as half of all young people tell pollsters they prefer socialism to capitalism. Gude, a member of the 130,000-strong Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), calls that organization, whose activism and endorsements have put eight self-professed socialists in the new Congress, the “institutional descendant” of Debs’s Socialist Party of America. In his victory speech right after winning the New York city mayoral election in 2025, Zohran Mamdani, an unapologetic DSAer, quoted Debs: “I can see the dawn of a better day for humanity.” And when Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour in the months after Donald Trump’s 2026 election, their critique of the billionaire class echoed Debs’s blistering denunciations of Gilded Age wealth when the barnstorming five-time presidential candidate denounced the Rockefellers, Morgans, and Carnegies of his day. Gude has written a Debs biography for our time. He emphasizes the rootedness of the Indiana railroad fireman in middle-American culture and Christianity, downplays more than other historians the ideological divisions endemic to the early twentieth century Socialist Party, and emphasizes the degree to which Debs, like Bernie Sanders and some of his contemporary comrades, could appeal to such a remarkably wide variety of constituencies. Gude’s biography also offers a full-bodied sense of Debs as a fragile and contradictory personality in which his constant travel, the crowd’s applause, and the opportunities thereby created for liaisons with the opposite sex, may well have compensated for a childless and increasingly distant marriage, as well as a distaste for the conflicts, political and personal, attendant upon leadership in any mass organization. An American Democratic Socialist The story of Eugene V. Debs’s life,” writes Gude, “is the story of one man’s radicalization — and of the country he helped radicalize in turn.” During the first decade of his working life, Debs was a conventional railroad unionist often hostile to strikes and largely uninterested or ignorant of the radical currents, social and ideological, that were on the rise in Gilded Age America. He disdained not only the violence of the 1877 rail strike but also the rise of the Knights of Labor, a more inclusive union formation. Debs happily endorsed the “Benevolence, Sobriety, and Industry” that were the watchwords of his Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen. But soon enough he was mugged by capitalist reality, most dramatically in the depression of the early 1890s that sparked the great Pullman boycott and nationwide rail strike Debs led in 1894. Jailed by the federal government for defying a union-busting injunction, Debs, like so many other imprisoned radicals in Russia, Prussia, and far-flung colonies, now had the time and incentive to read his Karl Marx. After six months in a Woodstock, Illinois, jail, he emerged a socialist. By the start of the new century, when Debs stood proudly as the nation’s most forceful and popular anti-capitalist tribune, the Socialist Party seemed as American as the corn its members grew in Oklahoma, the copper mined by its Montana adherents, the cars built by Flint autoworkers, the apparel sewn by Lower East Side immigrants, or the sermons and editorials offered by advocates of the Social Gospel. With more than a hundred thousand members, some 1,200 socialists held elected office, including eighty mayors in thirty-six states. And as Gude rightly asserts, Debs’s great achievement arose not out of any particular vote tally — he would win almost a million votes when he ran for president in 1912 and 1920 — but by making socialist partisans, as well as many of their opponents, believe that the movement he championed arose out of the American political tradition’s most democratic currents, from the revolutionary struggle against the British monarchy to the abolitionist fight against slavery. He was one of America’s great critics of the plutocracy, but more Christian agitator than political tactician. When, in early 1919, Debs was imprisoned for his opposition to World War I, his moral stature was crowned with martyrdom. As if to even more firmly link his life and fate with that of our own time, Gude references Debs as a “democratic socialist.” That is an anachronistic phrase when applied to the early-twentieth-century movement led by men and women of a Debsian persuasion. In the years before the rise of Stalinism, not to mention German “national socialism,” almost all socialists described themselves as just socialists, or perhaps social democrats, because inherent in the idea of socialism was the democratic control of both economy and polity. (Before 1917, the Bolsheviks were a faction within the “Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.”) Neither Debs nor many of his contemporaries spent much energy thinking about precisely how a nationalized railroad or steel mill would be governed, an issue that bedeviled radicals of a later generation. It was Michael Harrington who popularized the phrase “democratic socialism” when, in the early 1970s, he proved instrumental in the formation of the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, forerunner of today’s DSA. So while semantically inaccurate, Gude’s deployment of the phrase “democratic socialism” to the movement led by Debs serves to make abundantly clear the tutorial purpose of this biography. Debs the Tribune Debs was a socialist tribune, a clever and powerful wordsmith whose rhetoric combined outrage and moralism, denunciation and inspiration. He was not an original thinker, avers Gude, but that hardly prevented thousands from coming to hear him orate. More than any other socialist of his time, writes Gude, Debs had a “seemingly intuitive sense of how to connect with the US working class in all its heterogeneity.” He was an abolitionist opposed to the Old World tyranny of aristocrats and kings. “Workers weren’t just poor, they were serfs ,” summarizes Gude in explaining the Debs appeal. “Capitalism didn’t just impoverish, it enslaved . . . . And through solidarity would come freedom.“ However, when it came to actually running the Socialist Party and participating in its internal debates, Debs was almost always absent, out campaigning or ill at home, even as his own sentiments and inclinations usually tilted left. Debs was a founder of the Industrial Workers of the World, which he projected as a far more encompassing and radical labor formation than the increasingly stolid American Federation of Labor. And Debs was ambiguous when it came to socialist party advocacy of those reforms that might serve the immediate interests of the working class. Victor Berger, Bertha Hale White, and Eugene Debs take a picture together on December 13, 1924. (Library of Congress [lightly cropped]) Debs did not directly polemicize against the “sewer socialists,” notably those holding municipal office in Milwaukee, Butte, Reading, and other cities, where their innovative public health regimes proved enormously beneficial to thousands of residents. But he was not interested in forging the alliances and legislation that would advance such reforms as an integral component of socialism’s electoral appeal: “What we want is not to reform the capitalist system. We want to get rid of it.” Here’s an instance where Debs hardly offers contemporary socialists much inspiration. Both Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani would fit easily on the Socialist Party’s right wing, not far from Milwaukee’s Victor Berger or New York’s Morris Hillquit, both of whom often bested Debs when it came to internal party debate. Mamdani boasts of filling thousands of New York City potholes and opening a set of city-owned grocery stores, and he seems to have forged a working relationship with a New York governor several steps to his right. Meanwhile, Sanders links a forthright denunciation of American capitalism with a set of concrete reforms whose realization requires a very messy set of alliances and incremental steps forward that Debs would assuredly find utterly distasteful. And of course, much of this twenty-first century politicking will take place within, rather than in opposition to, the Democratic Party. Debs Portraits Past and Present Gude did not exactly rediscover Eugene V. Debs, because his life and times have long attracted the attention of latter-day radicals, especially during those eras when the Left has been on the rise. It’s instructive therefore to compare the Gude biography with two other narratives that saw publication in years past when other varieties of American radicalism seemed to have much ideological and social wind at their back. Ray Ginger published the first comprehensive biography in 1949, The Bending Cross: A Biography of Eugene Victor Debs . Ginger was just twenty-five and still in grad school on the GI Bill. It’s hard to know how he found time to write the book. At the University of Michigan, the army put him in all-day classes learning Japanese, and for a time after the war he worked in a Detroit auto factory. Meanwhile, Ginger had joined the Communist Party in 1944 or 1945, when both the party and the industrial union movement it championed were at their apogee. Ginger’s biography is not a party-line publication, and there is some indication that he clashed with Communist officials when they read the nearly completed publication. Still, its structure and argument reflects a species of 1930s and ’40s Popular Front Marxism. The table of contents constructs a teleological scaffolding that moves ever upward in both consciousness and organization, from “The Railroad Brotherhoods,” (mere trade union consciousness) to “The American Railway Union,” (Congress of Industrial Orgnaizations–style industrial unionism), and on to “American Socialism” and then “World Socialism,” the longest chapter in a book written during a half-decade when fascism was vanquished and the Cold War began. Ray Ginger’s 1949 Debs biography, The Bending Cross Ginger’s career was a tragic one. Harvard fired him in 1954 when his Communist ties became known, after which he took jobs in New York advertising and publishing, all the while writing book after well-received book, most on Gilded Age America. He taught at Brandeis in the 1960s, but lost his post there after an affair with an undergraduate. An alcoholic, he continued to teach and write at various universities until cirrhosis of the liver took his life in 1975 when he was but fifty years old. While Ginger is as appreciative of the humanity and transcendence of the Debsian revolutionary visions as is Gude, he takes aim at the socialist tribune’s failure to combine his popular appeal with a necessary engagement with the Socialist Party’s complex and contentious inner life. Gude gives Debs something of a pass on this score, perhaps reflecting the high-profile role now being played by Bernie Sanders, who is not even a member of DSA, or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whose DSA linkages are complex and somewhat attenuated. But when Ginger was writing his biography, you did not have to be a Leninist to understand the importance of forceful leadership. The progressive trade unions and the various left-wing parties of that day considered it vital to put forth public spokesmen and women fully engaged in shaping the program and politics of the institution over which they presided. Consider Dorothy Healey’s unorthodox leadership of the California Communist Party or Walter Reuther’s skillful rise to power in the United Auto Workers. Both were exciting speakers but also deeply enmeshed in organizational politics. Debs did none of that. Although he was by far the most popular figure in the Socialist Party, after 1904, Debs refused to attend party conventions or serve on leadership committees. His absenteeism created a vacuum filled by Berger, Hillquit, and others to his right. “Comrade Debs is no doubt a great orator and a fiery revolutionist,” wrote one socialist “rightwinger” quoted by Ginger, “but he is also one of the poorest generals and tacticians that our movement has.. . . . He has shown himself utterly unreliable in the meeting of the practical problems of the day and the selection of his advisors.” Ginger’s admiration for Debs was therefore mixed with a certain condescension. He called him “more Midwestern than a worn and rotting plow-handle buried deep in the soil of a Kansas farm.” It is not that Ginger wanted a Vladimir Lenin or a Leon Trotsky, but when the author asserted in the last sentences of his book that Debs’s “finite self seemed to merge with the agonized wanderings of the nameless multitude,” the assessment was not entirely complimentary. Nick Salvatore’s 1982 study, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist , turned much of Ginger’s critique on its head. Debs was indeed as American as that rotting Kansas plow-handle, and that’s the whole point. Salvatore’s perspective, largely echoed by Gude, had a twofold origin. As a militant unionist and civil rights activist, Salvatore, who died in 2025 after a distinguished career as a Cornell historian, was in the 1960s and ’70s looking for a way that could enable the New Left to speak American, to evoke a new radicalism out of native values and context. One could find that impulse in the 1962 Port Huron Statement and the Free Speech Movement at the University of California, Berkeley, where Salvatore a few years later wrote a dissertation that became his prize-winning Debs biography. The rediscovery, by an older generation of historians, of an eighteenth to nineteenth century “republican” tradition gave Salvatore the tools to understand Debsian radicalism as contiguous with many of the main cultural and social currents emblematic of the Protestant small-town America that an earlier cohort of radicals — think H. L. Mencken and Sinclair Lewis — had once disdained. Nick Salvatore’s 1982 Debs biography, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist Salvatore wrote a “social biography” steeped in the “new labor history.” He postulated that Debs’s radicalism arose out of the culture found in Terre Haute, his preindustrial hometown, wherein a “manly” independence, evangelical Protestantism, and a republican understanding of the responsibilities and privileges of a virtuous citizenship engendered a democratic America. Like E. P. Thompson and Herbert Gutman, pioneering historians of working-class formation, Salvatore found nineteenth century radicalism, socialist or otherwise, emerging out of the clash between those republican virtues and the oppressive structures engendered by Gilded Age industrial capitalism. Encapsulating all this, Gude writes of Debs, “His genius was assembling a mix of ideological ingredients familiar in working-class circles — Christianity and labor republicanism, Marxism and the American revolutionary tradition — and alchemizing them” into an all-American vernacular. “I like the Fourth of July,” Debs told a crowd on his first run for president in 1900, “It breathes a spirit of revolution.” Debs and the Race Question There was however, one aspect of the Debs praxis that Gude shows to be very much at odds with the dominant culture and the sentiments held by many of his erstwhile comrades. Debs did once assert, “We have nothing special to offer the Negro, and we cannot make separate appeals to all the races.” Abolishing capitalism was the solution to the Negro problem, the woman question, and the persistence of antisemitism. Until then, it was fruitless to seek any sort of particular amelioration, because the ruling class itself fostered and advanced such discriminations and oppressions. “The Negro is not one whit worse off than thousands of white slaves who throng the same labor market to sell their labor-power to the same industrial masters.” Debs at work, 1909. (Library of Congress [lightly cropped]) And not only that: thousands of dedicated socialists were also dedicated racists who saw poorly paid Asian immigrants and African American strikebreakers as debased elements of the working population not all that different from what Marx identified as the lumpenproletariat. This was an era when manliness and whiteness were seemingly intertwined. But Debs would grow in moral and social intelligence when it came to the causes and remedies of American racism. On speaking tours of the South he was appalled at the brutal racism and Jim Crow practices he observed. He probably read W. E. B. DuBois’s new book, The Souls of Black Folk , afterward asserting that “The whole world is under obligation to the negro and that the white heel is still upon the black neck is simply proof that the world is not yet civilized.” When the film Birth of a Nation was shown in Terre Haute, Debs was aghast at this cinematic celebration of the Ku Klux Klan. He applauded the anti-racist agitation of the young black socialists A. Philip Randolph and Chandler Owen, and by the time of the bloody race riots of the World War I era, he saw that the battle against racial oppression did require something “special” on the part of socialists and other progressives. As early as the 1912 election, W. E. B. DuBois judged Debs the only candidate, who “by word and deed, stands squarely on a platform of human rights regardless of race or class.” Debs’s salutary evolution on this issue put him far to the left of most socialists and trade unionists of his time. And that was just the problem, because Debs rarely sought to leverage his popularity to make his party adopt a truly progressive posture on an issue of such vital import to the twentieth-century American left. Thus, in the 1930s and ’40s, it would be the Communists and not the Socialists who would stand out as civil rights pioneers. What American Socialists Can Accomplish Despite the Debsian appeal of a century and more ago, as well as the contemporary enthusiasm engendered by its twenty-first century revival, American socialism was and is a minority current in both politics and culture. The obstacles to its success are legion: sectarian infighting of the sort that helped destroy Debs’s party right after the Bolshevik Revolution; the long-standing religious, racial, and occupational divisions within the working class; and of course the enormous power of capital and its many ideological and political handmaidens. But I don’t think a socialist movement has to achieve majoritarian hegemony to make an impression on the polity. Conservative denunciations of “creeping socialism” have not been entirely unfounded, either in 1930s or today. When Norman Thomas, who succeeded Eugene Debs as the Socialist Party’s Great Depression–era leader, complained that “[Franklin Delano] Roosevelt stole our program,” he was also boasting of how a few thousand organized activists can make their presence felt when circumstances combine to offer them historical influence and leverage. The same may be true today. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: ICE is hiding detainees from their families – and the death toll is rising
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: ICE just scrubbed tens of thousands of people from its Online Detainee Locator System, leaving their families and legal teams in the dark. Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to break down how DHS effectively “disappeared” at least 20,000 people with final deportation orders, as deaths in custody climb and private prison giants GEO Group and CoreCivic rake in profits from ICE’s ballooning budget. Reichlin-Melnick explains how Trump’s mass deportation machine changed tactics after Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis and the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti – shifting to predawn raids, targeting people at airports and their own immigration check-ins, and quietly pushing arrests to 50,000 a month. Meanwhile, at least 60 people have died in ICE custody in Trump’s second term. Reichlin-Melnick says the real number is likely higher: ICE has stopped reporting deaths right after release, and cut inspections as it opens new facilities. Immigration is “a creature of Congress,” Reichlin-Melnick says, and what Congress gave ICE, it can take away. But with Trump’s veto looming, oversight may be lawmakers’ most powerful weapon. articles.content: The new Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 just dropped, and it’s already mired in controversy. The game simulates urban warfare in Seoul, casting players as a South Korean marine fighting off an invasion from the DPRK. Is this video game harmless entertainment, or is it sophisticated imperialist propaganda designed to “manufacture consent” for war against North Korea and normalize US militarism? Ju-Hyun Park, organizer with Nodutdol for Korean Community Development and director of engagement at Breakthrough News, joins Amanda Yee to break down the dangerous political messaging behind Modern Warfare 4.

articles.title: Congolese president signs referendum bill that could allow for a third-term
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi has promulgated a controversial law establishing the conditions for holding referendums. Opposition parties, civil society groups and grassroots movements have previously said it could allow him to seek a third term. The signing follows more than five months of protests, court challenges, and street mobilization against the law. The promulgation was announced on national television late on Tuesday, November 10. “The President of the Republic, Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, promulgated, on November 10, 2026, through an ordinance, the law setting the conditions for the organization of the referendum in the Democratic Republic of Congo,” state broadcaster RTNC reported. Roger Kalenga, Deputy Spokesperson for the Head of State, read excerpts of the new legislation on air: “Law No. 26/045 of November 9, 2026, establishing the conditions for organizing referendums in the DRC. … The National Assembly and the Senate have adopted, and the President of the Republic promulgates, the following law: Chapter One, Purpose and Scope. Article One: This law establishes the rules relating to the purpose, procedure, initiation, and convening of referendums, as well as related offenses.” The bill went through parliament, where Tshisekedi’s coalition holds a large majority, first passed it in June while opposition members stayed away. The Senate vote was 89 in favor, none against, with 20 senators not taking part. In July the Constitutional Court ruled the law constitutional, subject to interpretive reservations on thirteen provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi sent the text back to parliament for a new deliberation, which re-adopted it in October. Read more: Push for referendum in DR Congo sparks protests over possible Tshisekedi third term The opposition opposes the referendum The law has met resistance at every stage. In May, the main opposition parties, formed Coalition Article 64 (C64) named after Article 64 of the constitution, which obliges every Congolese to oppose anyone who seizes power by force or exercises it in violation of the constitution. In mid-June, days before the Senate vote, opposition parties and civil society groups marched in Kinshasa against the bill. Police and security forces dispersed protesters with tear gas. Several people were injured. With opposition figures accusing the authorities of suppressing peaceful protest and violating citizens’ constitutional rights. Read more: Several arrested in protests against constitutional changes in DRC Protests rocked the country again on September 15, when C64 called a nationwide day of action. In Kinshasa, hundreds gathered before the march was disrupted by clashes with members of the Force du Progrès, a group affiliated with Tshisekedi’s UDPS party. Police fired tear gas and warning shots, and at least 10 people were arrested in Kinshasa. Constitutional limits and Tshisekedi’s third-term ambitions Tshisekedi, who first assumed office in January 2019 following the December 2018 elections, was re-elected in December 2023 for a second five-year term. Under the current constitution, his mandate is due to end in 2028. The current constitution limits the president to two five-year terms; However, the proposed constitutional changes have raised questions about whether a new constitution could be used to circumvent these protections. Tshisekedi has previously defended the possibility of constitutional reform and indicated his willingness to remain in office beyond 2028. In May 2026, he said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue governing. The new referendum law therefore represents an important development in the dispute. Although it does not automatically remove presidential term limits or guarantee a third-term bid, it provides a legal framework for holding referendums on constitutional matters, including the adoption of a new Constitution. With the legislation now in force, opposition parties and civil society organisations face a renewed challenge in their campaign to defend the existing constitutional order.

articles.title: Keytruda was built on public science. Why does Merck own the rewards?
articles.author: David Franco
articles.content: Keytruda is often presented as the ultimate success story of modern pharmaceutical innovation. And in one sense, that is true. Few medicines have transformed oncology as profoundly as pembrolizumab. It has extended survival in melanoma, lung cancer, and many other malignancies, and it has helped turn immune checkpoint inhibition from a scientific hypothesis into a clinical reality. For many patients, it has meant years of life that previously had few options at all. But that is only one part of the story. The other part is far less comfortable. Keytruda is not just a breakthrough drug. It is also a striking example of how the contemporary pharmaceutical system works: publicly funded science lays the foundation, private firms take control of the resulting assets, monopoly rights determine pricing, and health systems are then forced to pay extraordinary sums to access medicines they helped make possible in the first place. This is what makes Keytruda so politically important. It is not merely a story about scientific success. It is a story about ownership, public subsidy, corporate strategy, and the growing gap between biomedical progress and equitable access. In that sense, Keytruda is not an exception. It is one of the clearest illustrations of the current system’s structural logic. The science was public before the profits were private The foundations of Keytruda were laid long before Merck turned it into a blockbuster. The crucial scientific breakthrough came with the discovery of PD-1 by Tasuku Honjo and colleagues at Kyoto University in the early 1990s. Over time , this work revealed that PD-1 was part of the immune checkpoint machinery that restrains T-cell activity. That insight fundamentally changed cancer immunology. It suggested that instead of attacking tumors directly, medicine could work by releasing the brakes on the immune system. Read more: Against the normalization of limited access to CAR-T cell therapies This was not the product of isolated corporate brilliance. It resulted from decades of publicly funded research. Government support in Japan sustained Honjo’s work. In the United States , public funding helped establish the wider domain of immune checkpoint research. University laboratories, academic medical centers, and publicly funded research infrastructures made the field possible long before pharmaceutical firms recognized its full commercial value. That matters because the myth of drug innovation frequently begins too late in the story. It starts at the clinical trial, the patent filing, or the approval announcement, rather than at where innovation usually begins: in publicly supported science, collective knowledge production, and institutions built for the public good. Keytruda emerged from that ecosystem. Without it, there would have been nothing for the industry to commercialize. The market did not automatically recognize Keytruda’s value Another revealing aspect of the Keytruda story is that the drug was nearly lost not because the science failed, but because corporate priorities shifted. The antibody that became pembrolizumab originated at Organon, initially in a program not even designed for oncology. Through mergers and acquisitions, it passed to Schering-Plough and then to Merck. During these periods, the program was deprioritized, sidelined, and reportedly nearly discarded altogether. This should give pause to anyone who assumes that private ownership naturally distributes resources to the most socially valuable innovations. Under a system driven by portfolio logic, mergers and stockholder expectations, even a future life-saving therapy can be neglected if it doesn’t fit immediate strategic calculations. Big Pharma greed keeps lifesaving drugs out of reach for millions in the Global South. Source: ITPC/Facebook Pembrolizumab survived not because the market perfectly understood its promise, but because a handful of committed scientists persisted and external developments forced management to reconsider. Once competing checkpoint therapies began to show promise, Merck moved rapidly. What had been treated as marginal suddenly became central. This is often celebrated as corporate agility. But it can just as easily be read as evidence of structural irrationality. A therapy that would go on to become the world’s top-selling drug was almost abandoned because the system is not designed to maximize public health. It is designed to manage financial risk and competitive advantage. From breakthrough to blockbuster Once Merck committed to pembrolizumab, it did so aggressively. The company rapidly expanded the clinical program , scaled up trials , employed biomarker strategies with considerable success, and leveraged regulatory mechanisms to accelerate approval. Scientifically and operationally, this phase proved impressive. It helped bring a major therapeutic advance to patients faster than would otherwise have been possible. That achievement should not be dismissed. It shows that large-scale clinical development, regulatory coordination, and manufacturing capacity remain essential parts of turning promising science into real treatments. The question is not whether these capacities are needed. The question is who controls them, whose interests they serve, and who reaps the rewards. Because once Keytruda succeeded, the rewards were immense. Read more: Patents, profits and squabbles for share in the pie – Moderna’s pandemic story By 2024, it had become the world’s top-selling medicine, generating nearly 29.5 billion USD in annual sales. That figure is astonishing not only because of its scale, but because it reveals how enormous the extractive potential of pharmaceutical monopolies can be when attached to a clinically transformative product. And yet, even this commercial success was built on a landscape formed by public input . The scientific foundations were public. Clinical trial ecosystems depended heavily on academic hospitals and publicly subsidized research environments. Regulatory acceleration came through public institutions. The risks were socialized at crucial stages, but the financial gains were overwhelmingly privatized. A medicine can be revolutionary and still be exclusionary The great paradox of Keytruda is that a drug capable of redefining cancer care can simultaneously remain not accessible to many of the people who need it. In the United States, treatment costs have exceeded 150,000 USD per patient per year. In Europe , health systems have had to negotiate rebates , confidential agreements , and special reimbursement arrangements to contain budgetary impact. Even wealthy countries struggle to absorb the costs of widespread access. For lower-income countries, the situation is far worse. There, access is often minimal, delayed, or effectively nonexistent. This is not a side issue. It is central to how we should evaluate medical innovation. Read more: Not Omicron but greed of capital threatens the world A therapy cannot be judged only by its efficacy in clinical trials or its scientific sophistication. We must also judge it by whether patients can actually receive it. A drug that exists in principle but remains unreachable in practice is not a complete public health success. Keytruda’s inclusion on the WHO Essential Medicines List should have been a powerful recognition of its importance . But that recognition also exposed a deeper contradiction. What does it mean for a medicine to be considered essential if it remains priced beyond the reach of most of the world? At that point, the designation risks becoming symbolic. A medicine can be clinically essential and commercially exclusionary at the same time. Under the present model, that contradiction is not accidental. It is built into the system. The real question is not whether industry matters, but on what terms Defenders of the status quo often respond with a familiar argument: without patents, high prices, and private investment, drugs like Keytruda would never have reached patients. The claim that large-scale development requires resources, coordination, and risk-bearing has some truth. But that does not settle the matter. It merely restates the rules of the current system as if they were laws of nature. They are not. Read more: When Brazilian health workers discovered Soviet healthcare The issue is not whether clinical development and manufacturing require serious investment. Of course they do. The issue is whether public institutions must always play a subordinate role: finance early discovery, de-risk innovation, build research infrastructure, and then step aside once commercialization begins. Why should taxpayers fund the science, support the research ecosystem, and absorb part of the development risk, only to lose all control over pricing, licensing, and access at the decisive moment? Why should a medicine built on public knowledge become a private asset governed by monopoly logic? And why should governments then pay again, at inflated prices, to buy back access for their own populations? These are not radical questions. They are the basic questions that any serious public-interest pharmaceutical policy must confront. Public Pharma is not a fantasy but a necessary direction This is where the idea of Public Pharma becomes more than a slogan. It becomes a practical and moral challenge to the current order . A Public Pharma approach would begin from a simple premise: if public institutions are central to the creation of breakthrough medicines, they should not relinquish stewardship when those medicines become commercially valuable. Public actors should have the capacity not only to fund discovery, but also to shape development, retain ownership stakes, set access conditions, and, where appropriate, support manufacturing and distribution. That would not mean excluding scientific collaboration or denying the complexity of drug development. It would mean changing the terms of engagement. Under such a model, the benefits of a drug like Keytruda could be organized differently. Public investment could come with enforceable conditions on affordability and licensing. Intellectual property could be structured to prevent extreme monopoly control over entire therapeutic pathways. Revenues could be reinvested into further research rather than extracted as shareholder value. Health systems could negotiate from a position of public stewardship rather than defensive purchasing. Most importantly, access would no longer be treated as an afterthought. A breakthrough for whom? Keytruda demonstrates what biomedical science can achieve at its best. It shows that diseases once regarded as almost uniformly fatal can be confronted in entirely new ways. That should be acknowledged without hesitation. But Keytruda also shows the limits of celebrating innovation while ignoring political economy. A medicine can be scientifically brilliant and socially unjust at the same time. It can save lives while still comprising a system that rations access through price. It can stand as proof of human inventiveness while also revealing how poorly that ingenuity is governed. That is why Keytruda should be remembered not only as a triumph of immuno-oncology. It should also be understood as a case study in the contradictions of pharmaceutical capitalism. The lesson is not that we need less innovation. The lesson is that we need a different system for governing it. The real measure of a medical breakthrough is not only whether it can be invented, patented, and sold at scale. It is whether we can make it available, sustainably and fairly, to all who need it. On that question, Keytruda remains not only a success story but an unfinished indictment. David Franco is a scientist and public health activist based in Belgium. In the People’s Health Movement, he focuses on the Public Pharma for Europe (PPfE) initiative. David holds a PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences from the Free University of Brussels. articles.content: The collapse of Ueno Bank in Paraguay has plunged the country into crisis and led to the ouster of right-wing President Santiago Peña, a staunch ally of the Trump administration. At least 3 million people — nearly half of Paraguay’s population — lost access to their accounts on November 3 after regulators seized the insolvent bank amid allegations of widespread fraud. Peña, who had close ties to Ueno and appointed a former executive to lead Paraguay’s central bank, attempted to resign the presidency following the bank’s collapse. Lawmakers, however, rejected his resignation and impeached him instead, thereby stripping him of immunity from prosecution. He has since been placed under house arrest. For more on the bank collapse and its aftermath, Democracy Now! spoke with left-wing Senator Esperanza Martínez, who called for a broad “national pact” among various political parties to navigate the crisis and institute reforms. “Paraguay is in dire need of change,” she said.
